prompt: An analyst retypes OKONO's inventory with every capex and the limit as a count of USD where they were million USD, and changes nothing else. What changes in how the engine solves it, and where would the analyst see the change?
options: The optimizer switches to its fallback grid, since a limit in the hundreds of millions holds more partial portfolios than the exact solve allows.
The engine refuses the run with a PortfolioInputError, since a capex that large beside NPVs in million USD fails the engine's scale check.
Nothing in the solve or the output: the same funded set comes back, because the knapsack is exact at any scale.
The grid stays at 1 million USD per cell but every project now weighs a million times more cells, so none of them fits under the limit and nothing is funded at all.
explanation: Read at their typed precision, the retyped figures give the same knapsack scaled by a million, so OKONO still funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000. A unit slip is visible only in the inputs a reviewer reads.

prompt: A board minute says the optimizer picked the safe portfolio when it chose OKONO's 600.0000 set over its 450.0000 one. What role did the simulated loss probabilities play in selecting either set?
options: None: the optimizer and the frontier rank on risked EMV alone, and the seeded risk summary is computed afterwards for the set already chosen.
They broke a near tie, because the engine penalises each set's risked EMV by its simulated loss probability before comparing it with the rest of the frontier.
They screened the inventory, since any project whose failure branch lifts a set's P(loss) above the default is dropped before the knapsack runs.
They decided OK-3, which the simulation found worth its risk at 450.0000 and not worth it at 600.0000, where a safer set was available.
explanation: The 600.0000 set wins because 402.7500 beats every other set that fits; safety played no part, and a lower-risk set of nearly equal value is not offered.

prompt: OKONO's 450.0000 set totals 725.0000 of success-case NPV and its 600.0000 set only 473.0000. Why does the larger budget fund less success NPV?
options: The larger frontier is solved on a coarser grid, so the success cases of the funded projects are rounded down to whole cells before they are summed.
Success NPV is capped at the limit, so a larger budget spreads the same cap over more projects.
The optimizer at 600.0000 trades success NPV for a lower P(loss), which is why the safer set carries less upside than the riskier one.
OK-3 and its 420.0000 success case leave the set at 600.0000, and the optimizer maximises risked EMV, which rises to 402.7500.
explanation: Success NPV adds every best case as if all worked at once; risked EMV goes from 291.0000 to 402.7500 while success NPV falls, and only risked EMV is maximised.

prompt: A risky project's chance of success is left out of its row entirely. Beyond its risked EMV, what does the default do to the seeded risk summary of a set that funds it?
options: Nothing, since the simulation draws its own success rate from the entered percentiles whatever pos says, and only the optimizer uses the default.
The default of 1 travels into the simulation, so the project succeeds in every iteration, adds no failure to P(loss) and does not drag down the P90.
The simulation refuses to run for that set and reports P(loss) as null until a chance of success is entered for every funded project.
The simulation treats the blank as a coin toss and draws success half the time, so the set looks riskier than its risked EMV would suggest.
explanation: A pos left out or null is the default 1, used everywhere the project is used; at seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations the project is a certain success. A pos typed as a blank is refused by name before anything runs.

prompt: A study already paid for elsewhere is added to OKONO as a project with capex 0.0000 and a positive risked EMV, and the limit stays at 450.0000. Can the engine's answer hold it together with OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4?
options: No: the optimizer keeps the set it has already found for 450.0000 and adds nothing to a limit that is fully spent.
Yes, but only with overLimit true and overLimitBy of 1 million USD, since the engine lets a free project squeeze in over a limit that is already spent.
Yes: a project with capex 0.0000 weighs nothing on the exact solve, so it is funded beside OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 whenever its risked EMV is positive.
No, because a capex of 0.0000 is refused by the check that stops a negative capex.
explanation: On the exact solve a free project weighs nothing: freeProjectTightLimit funds free + A at capex 100.0000 for 70.0000 at a limit of 100.0000, and freeProjectZeroLimit funds the free project even at a limit of 0.0000.

prompt: The greedy walk down OKONO's EMV per million ranking at 450.0000 stops at OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5. Where does that set sit on the efficient frontier?
options: Below the frontier, since a set built from a ranking is always beaten at its own capex by some solved set of whole projects.
On point 11, level with the optimum, since both sets report the frontier's last value once rounding to cells is allowed for.
Nowhere, since the frontier records only sets that spend the whole limit, and the greedy set leaves 30.0000 of it unspent.
On point 10, the best set for 420.0000, one step short of the answer.
explanation: Point 10 is 420.0000 and 287.7500; the last step swaps OK-5 for OK-3 and adds 3.2500 for 30.0000 to reach 291.0000.

prompt: Two answers leave money idle: OKONO at 750.0000 spends 690.0000, and the gridUndershootFallback case, run on the stated fallback grid, spends 4500.0000 of 6000.0000. Why is only the second a reason to look harder at the set?
options: The second leaves a quarter of its limit idle and the first under a tenth, and the engine marks an answer unreliable once idle money passes a set share of the limit.
OKONO is solved exactly and its one left-out project, OK-6 at 310.0000, cannot fit, while the fallback rounds weights up and states optimalityGap 200.0000, the most its set may leave out.
The fallback reports overLimit true, which marks a grid problem, while OKONO at 750.0000 reports false and so needs no further check by the reader.
Both are equally suspect, since money left unspent always means the knapsack stopped early and a better set of whole projects exists somewhere.
explanation: On gridUndershootFallback the weights of 500, 500, 500 and 501 cells exceed 2000, so the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 with solveMethod grid-feasible, while W at 1499.0000 fits in money and the exact optimum is 860.0000. OKONO's 60.0000 is genuine because nothing that remains fits.

prompt: In tieDifferentComposition the engine returns A for 80.0000 where B + C also reaches 80.0000. What would a reviewer need in order to compare the P(loss) of the two sets?
options: A separate simulation of B + C, because the engine's risk summary covers only the set it returned and its output names no alternative optimum.
Nothing extra, since the risk summary averages P(loss) over every set that ties on risked EMV and reports the blended figure beside the funded set.
Nothing extra, since tied sets share their risked EMV and therefore share their P(loss) and their P90 as well, whatever projects they hold.
A rerun on a finer grid, since the engine lists alternative optima in its output only when the resolution drops below 1.0000.
explanation: Among sets tied on risked EMV the optimizer keeps the one with less capex, and at equal capex the set built without the later project in the list; A and B + C both cost 100.0000, so A comes back. A is one bet and B + C spreads the same 80.0000 over two, so their risk can differ widely.

prompt: Three inventories each hide a problem: a capex typed as -150, a pos typed as 1.4, and a large inventory sent to the stated fallback grid, which leaves out a project worth 200.0000. How does the engine treat each?
options: It refuses all three, because each one breaks a condition the knapsack needs before it can honestly return a set under the limit.
It refuses the first, reads the second as 1 and funds that project as a certain success, and flags the third through overLimit.
It refuses the first, reads the second as the default of 1, and reports the third as money unspent with nothing else beside it.
It refuses the first two by project name, and reports the third with solveMethod "grid-feasible" and an optimalityGap of 200.0000.
explanation: The messages read Project "B" has a negative capex (-150); capex must be 0 or more, and Project "a" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (1.4); pos must be a number from 0 to 1. On gridUndershootFallback the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 and states the bound beside it.

prompt: Working a graded inventory, a candidate finds the result reports solveMethod "grid-feasible". What does the Associate method require before the funded set is quoted?
options: Nothing extra, since the fallback rounds every weight up and a set that fits its grid can only be the exact optimum.
Rerun with a smaller limit until solveMethod reads "exact", since the engine offers its exact solve on request once asked.
Read its optimalityGap, 200.0000 on gridUndershootFallback, as the most risked EMV the set may leave out, and look for a left-out project that still fits in money.
Confirm overLimit reads false, since the fallback can only go wrong by overshooting the limit and the flag reports every overshoot.
explanation: The fallback rounds every weight up, so its set always fits the limit; it can fall short of the optimum, and optimalityGap states how far at most: 20.0000 on gridOvershootFallback, where nothing was lost, and 200.0000 on gridUndershootFallback, where W was left out.

prompt: A reviewer who counts rows from one opens an inventory without names or ids after a PortfolioInputError that blames Project "1" for a capex of -0.5. Which row holds the bad capex?
options: The first project in the list, since the engine numbers its rows from one in the same way the Suite's inventory table does.
The second project in the list, since an unnamed project is named by its position counted from zero.
Any project with a capex of -0.5, since the number in quotes counts the refused projects and names no position.
No row at all, since a capex of -0.5 rounds to zero cells and the message is a warning that the run continues past.
explanation: The message names a project by name, then id, then position from 0, and the check runs before any set is chosen, so no partial answer comes back.

prompt: A geologist enters OK-3's npv_p50 as 41.2500 because that is what the well is worth, and keeps pos at 0.250000 and fail_cost at 85.0000. What has gone wrong?
options: The well is risked twice, and with 0.750000 x 85.0000 now outweighing a quarter of 41.2500 its risked EMV turns negative, so it is never funded.
Nothing, since the engine sees a success case smaller than the fail cost and restores the entered npv_p10 of 700.0000 as the success case.
Only the spread moves, because npv_p10 and npv_p90 are rescaled around 41.2500, while the well's risked EMV of 41.2500 stays as entered.
The well is valued at 41.2500 as intended, because the optimizer reads npv_p50 directly and pos enters only the Monte Carlo draws.
explanation: npv_p50 is the success case, 420.0000 for OK-3, and the one line applies pos to it; a value already risked is discounted again and the failure branch dominates.

prompt: The workovers' two spread measures agree exactly and the exploration well's do not. What makes the well's mixture standard deviation the wider of its pair?
options: The mixture uses an explicit npv_stddev where one is entered, and OK-3 carries one while OK-5 falls back to its entered percentiles.
The success spread is taken from npv_p10 less npv_p90 and the mixture from npv_p10 less npv_p50, which is wider for a well with a long upside.
The mixture counts the drop from a success to a loss of 85.0000 three times in four, and OK-5 cannot fail, so it has no such drop.
The mixture adds the capex of 90.0000 as a second source of variance, and OK-5's capex is too small against its NPV to register.
explanation: The success spread describes the well only when it works, (700.0000 - 210.0000) / 2.5631 = 191.1747; failure widens the range, and fail costs set the floor of every simulated outcome.

prompt: Two rows enter percentiles of 200 and 50: one as npv_p10 200 and npv_p90 50, the other with the two swapped. Which row is more dangerous, and why?
options: The first, since its spread of 58.5229 exceeds the explicit 40.0000 the engine would prefer and so overstates the risk summary.
Neither, since the engine sorts the two percentiles before it divides, so both rows return a spread of 58.5229.
The swapped row, because the engine refuses inverted percentiles with a PortfolioInputError and the set can then not be solved at all.
The swapped row, whose spread of 0.0000 silently removes its success range from the risk summary.
explanation: In the right order the spread is (200 - 50) / 2.5631 = 58.5229; inverted, the published case returns 0.0000 with no error, because nothing checks that npv_p10 sits above npv_p90.

prompt: A greedy analyst funds OKONO straight down its ratio table until the money for 450.0000 runs out. Which candidate is the earliest one passed over, and why?
options: OK-3, since its 0.458333 is the lowest ratio and a greedy walk never reaches it.
OK-2, because after OK-1 and OK-4 reach 360.0000 its 180.0000 would take the total to 540.0000.
OK-6, because at 310.0000 it is the largest capex in the inventory and could not fit beside OK-1 at any stage of the walk.
OK-5, since after OK-1, OK-4 and OK-2 reach 540.0000 no room remains.
explanation: The walk then adds OK-5 for 420.0000, and neither OK-6 nor OK-3 fits the 30.0000 left, so it ends at 287.7500 against the optimizer's 291.0000.

prompt: A planner argues the greedy ranking must be sound because at 600.0000 it fills the budget exactly and matches the optimizer. What does that coincidence establish about other budgets?
options: That a ranking is exact whenever it spends the whole limit, which it misses at 450.0000 only because 30.0000 of that limit is left idle.
That the optimizer runs the ranking itself, so its 291.0000 at 450.0000 is a rounding artefact.
Nothing: the same ranking loses 3.2500 at 450.0000, and nothing in a ranking says in advance which budgets it will fill.
That the frontier's step ratios fall steadily past 450.0000, which is the condition under which a ranking always fills a budget.
explanation: At 600.0000 the walk funds OK-1, OK-4, OK-2 and OK-5 for 402.7500, the optimizer's own set; at 450.0000 it stops at 287.7500, and only solving the set tells the two budgets apart.

prompt: A licence commitment must be drilled although its risked EMV is negative. How does an analyst get it into OKONO's programme?
options: Take its capex off the limit before the run and optimise the rest, because the engine has no must-fund flag and never funds a project at 0 or less.
Raise the limit until the optimizer has room, since negativeEmvHugeBudget shows that a large enough budget eventually funds everything that fits.
Enter a pos of 1.4 so the clamp lifts it to certain success, which is the supported way to mark a project as mandatory.
Leave it in the inventory as it is, since the optimizer spends any unspent money on the next project whatever its value.
explanation: In negativeEmvHugeBudget a limit of 10000.0000 funds good + better for 120.0000 and still leaves the negative project out; funding it lowers expected value by exactly its negative EMV.

prompt: zeroEmvExcluded holds a project whose risked EMV is exactly 0.0000, under a limit of 500.0000 with room to spare. Why does the engine leave that project out?
options: The engine treats a risked EMV of exactly zero as a missing value and refuses the row before the knapsack starts.
The grid charges every project a cell, and a project worth zero can never win that cell against the good project.
It is an input error the engine corrected by a clamp, since any risked EMV below its fail cost is read as zero.
It adds nothing to the objective and would still use capex.
explanation: The engine funds good alone for 50.0000 and 30.0000; a project at 0 or less is never funded, and money may be left unspent.

prompt: An auditor wants to export the 60.0000 that OKONO's five-project answer at 750.0000 leaves idle. Which part of the engine's return carries it?
options: As overLimitBy with a negative sign, since that flag measures the distance between the funded capex and the limit on either side.
Nowhere as a field: the engine returns the limit, the set, its capex and its EMV, and the reader derives the unspent amount by subtraction.
As the resolution, which rises to 60.0000 whenever a limit cannot be spent exactly in whole projects on the exact grid.
As a partial slice of OK-6, which the engine funds with the leftover money and reports beside the five whole projects.
explanation: Every unspent figure is derived, 750.0000 - 690.0000 = 60.0000, and it is genuine because OK-6 alone costs 310.0000; the frontier's last point is printed at 690.0000, the capex its set costs.

prompt: tieIdenticalProjects funds twinA, and the golden accepts twinA or twinB. If the inventory is re-sorted so twinB is entered first, what should a reviewer expect?
options: twinA again, since ties are broken by the alphabetical order of project ids before the knapsack begins building sets.
Both twins, since a limit of 100.0000 holding two sets of 50.0000 funds the pair and reports 100.0000 of risked EMV.
twinB can come back instead, because the knapsack keeps the first best set it builds and an equal set found later never displaces it.
An error, since the engine refuses any inventory in which two different sets tie on the objective.
explanation: The output has no field for alternative optima, so entry order decides between tied sets; nothing in the inputs separates the twins at 50.0000.

prompt: A budget of 150.0000 is proposed for OKONO, halfway between the frontier points at 120.0000 and 180.0000. What is the best risked EMV it buys?
options: 89.7500, the lower point's value, since no whole set between those two capexes does better.
The midpoint of 89.7500 and 127.7500, read along the straight line the chart draws between those two frontier points.
127.7500, since OK-1 and OK-5 together fit once the budget passes the halfway mark between the points.
A share of the 38.0000 the next step adds, priced at that step's 0.633333 per extra million USD.
explanation: The frontier is a staircase of whole sets; every budget from 120.0000 to just short of 180.0000 buys exactly OK-1's 89.7500.

prompt: Step 3 of OKONO's frontier reads 1.616667 per extra million USD, while OK-1 earns 0.747917 per million of its own capex. Why are the two so different?
options: Step 3 counts OK-1's success-case NPV where the project ratio uses its risked EMV, so the step overstates the project.
Step 3 is measured in the frontier's cells while the project ratio uses million USD, and each cell there is worth more.
Step 3 adds OK-1 on top of OK-3, so its gain counts OK-3's risked EMV a second time beside OK-1's own.
Step 3 is the swap of OK-3 for OK-1, gaining 48.5000 for 30.0000.
explanation: 89.7500 less 41.2500 is 48.5000 over 120.0000 less 90.0000; only a step that adds a project on top reads as that project's ratio, as steps 4 and 10 show OK-5's 0.633333.

prompt: A reviewer sees the frontier's smallest gain recur on three separate steps and suspects the grid is repeating itself. What does each of those steps actually trade?
options: OK-3 added on top of a smaller set, its 41.2500 split across three budgets in the pieces the grid allows.
The same trade: OK-5 out and OK-3 in, 41.2500 less 38.0000 for 90.0000 less 60.0000.
Three different trades that coincide because every capex is a multiple of 30.0000.
A rounding step the exact grid inserts when no whole project fits.
explanation: At point 11 that swap turns the greedy set's 287.7500 into the optimum's 291.0000, so its ratio of 0.108333 does not mean the last 30.0000 was badly spent.

prompt: A sponsor offers OKONO a single extra million on top of the 450.0000 limit, citing the 0.733333 per extra million USD that the next frontier step reads. What does that million add?
options: 0.733333, the next step's ratio, bought a million at a time as the budget climbs toward the next point.
0.108333, the ratio of the step just taken, which is the best available estimate of what the next million returns.
0.0000 more, since the value stays at 291.0000 until the budget reaches 480.0000, where it steps to 313.0000.
A share of OK-5, whose 0.633333 per million is the cheapest way to put a small increment on top of the optimum.
explanation: The ratio 0.733333 is 22.0000 over 30.0000, an average across a whole step; no project is funded in part, so a million inside a step buys nothing.

prompt: Told to trim OKONO's 600.0000 programme back to 450.0000, a manager strikes the gas compression project and keeps the rest. How does the trimmed programme compare with re-solving?
options: It leaves OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5 at 420.0000 for 287.7500, 3.2500 short of the 291.0000 re-solving finds by bringing back OK-3.
It reaches the re-solved answer, because optimal sets are nested across budgets.
It beats re-solving, because the manager keeps OK-5, the one certain project, where the optimizer would trade it for a riskier well.
It matches the re-solved value with a different set, since both reach 291.0000 and the engine breaks such a tie by entry order.
explanation: No single drop from the 600.0000 set reaches the 450.0000 answer, because that answer holds OK-3, which the larger set left out.

prompt: Handed a raised budget of 600.0000, a manager tops up the solved 450.0000 set with whatever else fits and does not re-run the optimizer. Where does topping up stop?
options: At 402.7500, since adding in ratio order to a solved set reaches the next one.
At 329.0000 for 510.0000, with OK-5 added and nothing else fitting, against 402.7500 from solving again.
At 444.0000, with OK-2 and OK-5 both added, since the extra 150.0000 of budget covers the pair of them together.
At 291.0000, since the engine refuses a project added to a solved set by hand.
explanation: After OK-5 only 90.0000 is left and OK-2 costs 180.0000; the solved set at 600.0000 gives up OK-3 to fund OK-1 + OK-2 + OK-4 + OK-5.

prompt: Both OKONO frontiers pass through the same first dozen points up to 450.0000 and 291.0000. What does that agreement prove, and what does it leave unproven?
options: It shows the 600.0000 answer contains the 450.0000 answer, since the longer frontier is built by extending the shorter one.
It shows nothing, because the second frontier is solved on a coarser grid and agrees with the first only through rounding.
It shows the extra 150.0000 goes to the same projects in the same order, which is why the first points agree.
The best value at each budget nests; the winning set at the larger limit does not.
explanation: Both frontiers pass through 450.0000 and 291.0000, yet OK-3 is funded at 450.0000 and dropped at 600.0000, where OK-1 + OK-2 + OK-4 + OK-5 reach 402.7500.

prompt: A report shows OKONO's frontier ending at 450.0000 and 291.0000 beside a funded set worth 287.7500. What should the reader conclude?
options: The funded set is the greedy set and the frontier is the optimum, which the engine prints side by side so the loss can be seen.
The grid has undershot, and the 3.2500 between them is a project rounding left out.
The two were not run on the same inventory and limit, so find which input changed before quoting either.
The frontier includes projects the funded set excludes for risk, so its last point always sits a little above the set.
explanation: The last point is the best risked EMV inside the whole limit and must match the funded set; at 450.0000 both read OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000, solved exactly with solveMethod "exact".

prompt: gridOvershootFallback, run on the stated fallback grid, reports a resolution of 3.000000 at a limit of 6000.0000. What does a resolution measure?
options: The size of one capex cell in the money units entered, the limit divided into 2000 cells, reported only when the fallback grid runs.
The precision of the risked EMV, so the answer is reliable only to within 3.000000 million USD of the true optimum.
The number of cells the limit is divided into, which grows when the capexes are typed in larger units.
The standard error of the simulated P(loss), which the engine shrinks as the limit grows.
explanation: 6000.0000 over 2000 is 3.000000 million USD per cell, and every capex is rounded up to whole cells, A to 1334, B to 668 and C to 665. On an exact solve the resolution is null, because there is no grid.

prompt: On gridOvershootFallback the stated fallback grid runs at 3.000000 per cell against a limit of 6000.0000, with A at 4000.0000, B at 2002.0000 and C at 1995.0000. Why are A and B never funded together there?
options: The fallback funds at most two of any three projects, and keeps the pair with the lower total capex.
Every capex rounds up to whole cells, B to 668, so A's 1334 and B's 668 overflow the 2000 cells, and the fallback funds A + C for 780.0000.
The fallback refuses any project whose capex does not divide evenly by the resolution, and B's 2002.0000 is refused.
A is charged the minimum of one cell as a large project, so the grid undercounts it by nearly its whole capex of 4000.0000.
explanation: Rounding every weight up keeps any set that fits the grid inside the limit. The fallback funds A + C at 5995.0000, the exact optimum, with overLimit false and optimalityGap 20.0000.

prompt: gridOvershootFallback reports optimalityGap 20.0000 and gridUndershootFallback 200.0000. What does each gap say about the fallback's set?
options: Both mean the grid was coarse by that many cells, the figure recording how many capexes were rounded up.
Each is exactly the risked EMV the fallback lost, so the first case lost 20.0000 and the second lost 200.0000.
Each is the amount by which the funded capex sits over the limit, reported beside overLimit for the reader to subtract.
Each is an upper bound on what was left out: the first set is the exact optimum at 780.0000, while the second falls 200.0000 short.
explanation: optimalityGap is the optimum on the same grid with every weight rounded down, less the funded EMV. On gridOvershootFallback that bound admits A + B, yet A + C is the exact optimum; on gridUndershootFallback X + Y + Z at 660.0000 falls short of all four at 860.0000 by exactly the gap.

prompt: A capital committee cannot see why the four gridUndershoot candidates, whose capex totals 5999.0000 against a limit of 6000.0000, are never funded together on the stated fallback of gridUndershootFallback. What stops the fourth there?
options: The engine caps a funded set at three projects on a coarse grid, which keeps the knapsack inside its time budget.
Z's 1502.0000 is refused as over a per-project ceiling of 1500.0000, and the grid drops W with it as the least valuable.
On a cell of 3.000000 every capex rounds up, and the four rounded weights need more than the 2000 cells the limit holds.
The four together would overshoot in money, so the overshoot flag removes the cheapest project before the answer is reported.
explanation: W, X and Y weigh 500 cells each and Z 501, one cell more than 2000; the fallback funds X + Y + Z for 660.0000 and states optimalityGap 200.0000. Solved exactly, gridUndershoot funds all four for 860.0000.

prompt: Between freeProjectTightLimit and freeProjectSlack the only change is one extra million of limit, and both fund the free project and A. What does the extra million buy?
options: The free project's capex, which the engine rounds up from 0.0000 to 1 million USD whenever a limit allows it.
Nothing: both fund capex 100.0000 for 70.0000, and the extra 1.0000 is left unspent.
A change of method, since a limit of 101.0000 sends the solve to the fallback grid.
A tie the engine breaks by entry order, which the extra million settles in the free project's favour.
explanation: A free project weighs nothing on the exact solve, so it is funded at a limit of 100.0000 already; freeProjectSlack funds the same set at capex 100.0000 against 101.0000, leaving 1.0000 unspent.

prompt: An inventory is typed entirely in USD where million USD was meant. Why can a project-by-project check of risked EMV per million of capex never reveal the slip?
options: Both amounts sit in the same unit, so it cancels, and OK-1's 0.747917 would come out of a USD inventory unchanged.
The ratio prints to six decimals, which is too coarse to show a factor of a million between two inventories.
The engine converts USD to million USD before computing risked EMV, so every ratio is taken on corrected numbers.
The ratio divides by capex in grid cells, and a cell is the same size in either unit.
explanation: The engine holds no currency field, no unit field and no scale check, and the exact solve returns the same set in any unit, as the rawDollars case shows; a mixed inventory is the slip no ratio can catch.

prompt: A candidate project spends its capex over three years, most of it in the last one. How does the portfolio engine represent that phasing?
options: It discounts later years at a rate implied by npv_p50, so it weighs less.
It splits the project into one knapsack item per year, each funded whole.
It does not: capex is one amount spent in one period, and no time value is added beyond the NPVs entered.
It charges the full capex against the limit but only the first year's share against the grid, at one cell per year of spend.
explanation: Projects are funded whole with capex never phased; OKONO's 450.0000 limit is met by 120.0000 plus 90.0000 plus 240.0000 as single amounts.

prompt: OK-3 costs 90.0000 to fund and loses 85.0000 if it fails. A modeller leaves fail_cost blank on the grounds that the engine already knows the capex. What does the engine use?
options: The capex of 90.0000, since a missing fail cost defaults to the money spent.
A fail cost of 0, because fail_cost is typed and never inferred from capex, so the dry hole is valued as free.
The success-case NPV with its sign reversed, since failure is modelled as losing the prize the well was drilled for.
Nothing: the row is refused until a fail cost is entered, because the one line cannot be evaluated with a term missing.
explanation: A missing fail_cost defaults to 0; in missingNpvIsZero a typed fail_cost of 8 at pos 0.25 gives -6.0000, all of it from the failure branch.

prompt: An asset team wants the optimizer to favour the steadier of two look-alike wells whose rows match everywhere except entered percentiles running twice as wide on one. What does the knapsack do with the pair?
options: It prefers the narrower one, because the one line subtracts the success spread from npv_p50 before weighting it by pos.
It prefers the wider one, because a wider range raises npv_p10 and the one line counts upside above the success case.
It funds the two together as a hedge, since the knapsack spreads a limit across projects whose ranges differ.
As identical: the percentiles feed only the risk summary.
explanation: Risked EMV = pos x npv_p50 - (1 - pos) x fail_cost, so equal inputs give equal EMVs; where only one fits, entry order decides, as in tieIdenticalProjects.

prompt: A slide divides OFON-1's estimate at completion of 27600000 by OKONO's limit of 450.0000 to show the AFE's share of the capital programme. What is wrong with it?
options: The two models share nothing: OKONO is a capital inventory in million USD and OFON-1 an AFE in whole USD, so the ratio mixes units and describes no real programme.
Nothing is wrong, since both figures are amounts of planned spend, and a forecast from one model can be read against a limit from the other.
The estimate at completion should carry a P-label first, since it is a percentile of cost and must be named before any comparison.
The limit should be replaced by the 291.0000 of risked EMV, since a share of a programme is measured against its value.
explanation: This question examines the mix itself: OKONO's 450.0000 is million USD and OFON-1's 27600000 is USD, and the course never divides one model's numbers by the other's.

prompt: The Associate reading closes on OFON-1: as of 2027-08-15 its CPI is 1.009377 and its SPI 0.872063. Which of the two would read differently on a report dated another day inside the window?
options: CPI, because actual cost is read at the as-of date, while SPI is fixed once the progress on each line has been entered.
Both of them, since each index is a ratio to planned value and planned value is read from the calendar.
SPI, because planned value comes from the calendar, while CPI rests on an earned value of 15231500 that is the same at every as-of date.
Neither of them, since both indices are computed once when the AFE is created and stored against each line.
explanation: OFON-1 earns 15231500 at every as-of date with CPI 1.009377; SPI is 1.141290 at 2027-06-30 and 0.872063 at 2027-08-15.

prompt: A capstone answer writes P90 capex 450.0000, P90 NPV -18.3574 and P(loss) 0.123600. Which P-label is used correctly?
options: Only the P90 on the capex, since a capex is an estimate and estimates take the exceedance convention while outcomes do not.
Only the P90 on the NPV, the low case of simulated portfolio NPV at seed 20260829.
Both, since P90 names the value exceeded nine times in ten, cost or NPV.
Neither, since the engine's P90 is the high case of NPV.
explanation: This examines a mislabel: P-labels belong to a portfolio NPV outcome alone, with P90 the low case, and a capex, a limit or a probability never carries one.

prompt: Risking every row by hand before solving, a candidate's value for one project differs from the explorer's risked EMV column. What causes does the method name?
options: Grid rounding, since the column shows EMV after capex is rounded to cells.
The simulation, since the column reports the mean of the seeded Monte Carlo draws, which never lands exactly on the hand line.
Correlation, which the explorer applies to each project's EMV before printing.
A mistyped input, or a default that fired: a pos left out read as 1, or a negative fail_cost read as 0.
explanation: A pos over 1, under 0, blank or non-numeric never reaches the column, because it is refused by project name. OK-3's hand line, 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500, matching the engine shows the row was read as typed.

prompt: freeProjectZeroLimit and limitBelowEveryProject both run at a limit that no project with a cost can meet. Which of them returns a funded set, and why?
options: freeProjectZeroLimit, whose project costs 0.0000 and weighs nothing, so it is funded for 10.0000; below every project nothing fits.
limitBelowEveryProject, since a limit of 30.0000 funds part of A, and a fraction of a project is how a tight limit is used.
Both, since the engine relaxes a limit that no project can meet and funds the cheapest project it has.
Neither, since an empty set is the engine refusing a limit it cannot use, and no optimum exists for either input.
explanation: The engine funds the free project at a limit of 0.0000, which is the golden optimum; limitBelowEveryProject at 30.0000 funds nothing, capex 0.0000 and EMV 0.0000, because A costs 50.0000 and B 80.0000.

prompt: OKONO's gas compression project OK-2 is funded at a limit of 300.0000 million USD, left out at 450.0000 and funded again at 600.0000. What does that pattern say about how the engine chooses?
options: The engine ranks projects by risked EMV per million USD, and OK-2's place in that ranking moves because the limit changes the ratio it is scored on.
OK-2 was dropped at 450.0000 because the simulated loss probability of a set holding it crossed a ceiling the optimizer enforces on every run.
Each limit is solved on its own for the combination of whole projects with the largest summed risked EMV, so a project has no fixed place in a queue.
The run at 450.0000 fell back to a coarse grid that could not fit a capex of 180.0000, while the runs at the other two limits used the exact grid.
explanation: OK-2's ratio of risked EMV to capex is the same at every limit; what changes is what else the money buys, so at 450.0000 OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 returns 291.0000 without it.

prompt: OK-3 carries npv_p10 700.0000 and npv_p90 210.0000 beside its npv_p50 of 420.0000. What part do the two percentiles play in its risked EMV of 41.2500?
options: None: they set the success spread of 191.1747, which the engine uses only when it describes the risk of a funded set.
They replace npv_p50 when both are entered, since the engine takes the middle of the entered range as the success case before weighting it by pos.
They bound the success branch, holding pos x npv_p50 inside the entered range before the fail cost is taken off.
They scale the fail cost, since the engine reads the gap between them as the size of the loss on a dry well.
explanation: Risked EMV is pos x npv_p50 - (1 - pos) x fail_cost, so 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500 with no percentile in it; the spread is (700.0000 - 210.0000) / 2.5631.

prompt: The 450.0000 set carries a P(loss) of 0.123600 and the 600.0000 set a P(loss) of 0.001800. What part did those probabilities play in choosing each set?
options: They set a ceiling, so the optimizer rejected any set at 450.0000 whose simulated loss probability ran above 0.123600.
They broke near ties, so of two sets within one grid cell of each other the one less likely to lose money won.
They were weighted into the objective, so the exploration well entered the 450.0000 set only after a risk discount.
None, because the optimizer maximises summed risked EMV alone and the risk summary is computed afterwards for the set it already chose.
explanation: The optimizer never sees a probability: it funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000 at 450.0000, and a lower risk set of nearly equal value is never offered.

prompt: For the 450.0000 set the engine prints seed 20260829, iterations 10000, P(loss) 0.123600 and P90 -18.3574. Why does it show the seed?
options: Because the seed fixes the average correlation between projects, which is the one simulation input the risk summary has no other field to display.
So anyone can rerun the same simulation and reproduce its loss probability and percentiles exactly.
Because the loss probability is read from a normal approximation, and the seed records which version of that approximation the run applied.
Because the optimizer breaks ties with it, so another seed can fund another set.
explanation: The engine simulates success, failure and the success NPV of each project in every one of 10000 iterations from the seed, so the same seed and iterations reproduce P(loss) 0.123600 and P90 -18.3574 exactly.

prompt: For OKONO's 450.0000 set the risk summary reports P90 -18.3574 and P10 738.1043, in million USD. What is -18.3574?
options: The 90th percentile of simulated portfolio NPV, the value nine draws in ten fall below, which means the set most likely loses money.
The low case, the 10th percentile of simulated portfolio NPV under the exceedance convention.
The amount by which the set's capex could run over in a bad year, since a P90 on spending is the figure exceeded only one time in ten.
The normal approximation's low case, taken from an emv of 291.0000 and a stdDev of 271.6522, which the engine still prints beside the simulation.
explanation: P90 is the value nine outcomes in ten exceed, so it is the low case; the same set's P(loss) of 0.123600 confirms most draws are positive, and the percentiles are read from the seeded simulation.

prompt: An analyst types OKONO's limit of 450.0000 million USD and every capex as counts of USD, keeping the NPVs in million USD. What in the output shows that anything changed?
options: A PortfolioInputError, since a capex in the hundreds of millions is outside the range the engine accepts and nothing is chosen.
A unit warning, since the engine compares the limit with the NPVs and flags an inventory typed at the wrong scale.
The solveMethod, which reads "grid-feasible" once the capex is typed in USD, since figures that large leave the exact solve.
Nothing: solved exactly on the capex as typed, it funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 again with solveMethod "exact", and the engine holds no unit field.
explanation: The published rawDollars case does the same with the classic inventory: limit 450000000.0000, A + B + D for 250.0000, solveMethod exact. The engine holds no currency or unit field, so a consistently scaled capex column is invisible and harmless.

prompt: One OKONO row has its capex typed in USD while its npv_p50 stays in million USD, beside five rows typed consistently. What does the engine do?
options: It optimises without an error, and the project, whose capex now looks a million times too large, simply never fits.
It refuses the run with a PortfolioInputError, since a capex out of scale with its own NPV is caught by the same check that catches a negative capex.
It rescales the row, reading the Suite's million USD column label as a unit field to convert entries into.
It funds the project at every limit, since so large a capex tops the ranking by risked EMV per million USD.
explanation: The only refusal is a negative capex; the engine adds whatever it is given, and a limit such as 1000.0000 cannot hold a capex typed a million times too large.

prompt: The engine refuses an inventory with the message: Project "1" has a negative capex (-0.5); capex must be 0 or more. The project has no name and no id. Which row does a user counting rows from one have to fix?
options: The first row, since the engine numbers projects from one in its messages so that they match the row numbers the Suite shows beside the inventory.
Every row whose capex is below 1, since the message reports the smallest capex found and the number in quotes counts how many rows offend.
The second row, because with no name and no id the engine names the project by its position counted from 0.
No row yet, since the check runs after a set is chosen and names a project dropped from it.
explanation: The message uses the name, then the id, then the position from 0, so "1" is the second project; the check runs before any set is chosen and no partial answer comes back.

prompt: Why does the engine refuse a capex of -150 outright, with no clamp to 0?
options: A negative capex turns the risked EMV negative, and the engine refuses any project whose risked EMV is 0 or less, the same way it refuses a negative capex.
The knapsack grid cannot store a negative weight, so the refusal protects the array the optimizer builds and says nothing about what the input means.
A clamp to 0 would charge the project a grid cell for nothing, and the engine refuses every input that would take capacity the project never asked for.
A project that pays you to fund it breaks the idea of a limit.
explanation: Capex never enters the risked EMV line, and a project with EMV of 0 or less is simply left out. The published message reads Project "B" has a negative capex (-150); capex must be 0 or more.

prompt: A one in four exploration well has its chance of success typed correctly and its fail cost typed with a minus sign to show it is a loss. The run returns no error. How is the failure branch valued?
options: At nothing: a negative fail cost is read as 0, so a well like OK-3 would carry 105.0000, its success branch alone.
At twice the fail cost, since the minus sign typed in the field and the minus sign in the formula compound.
At its intended cost, because the engine takes the absolute value of a negative fail cost before it weights the branch.
It is never valued, since a negative fail cost is refused with the same error as a negative capex.
explanation: negativeFailCostIsZero returns 40.0000 for a fail cost of -30 at pos 0.5 on an npv_p50 of 80, the success branch alone. A pos typed as a percentage is caught: Project "Appraisal" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (30); pos must be a number from 0 to 1.

prompt: Four inventories are run through the optimizer. Which one does the engine refuse outright?
options: One with a limit of 30.0000 that sits under every project, since no set can be built and the knapsack has nothing it can return.
One holding a project whose npv_p10 is entered below its npv_p90, since a success spread cannot be built from an inverted range.
One holding a project with a capex of -0.5.
One holding a project with fail_cost -30, since a loss typed below zero is outside the range the engine documents for fail_cost.
explanation: The negative capex is refused: Project "1" has a negative capex (-0.5); capex must be 0 or more. limitBelowEveryProject at 30.0000 funds nothing, inverted percentiles give a spread of 0.0000, and a fail_cost of -30 is read as 0.

prompt: The published gridOvershoot case has projects costing 4000.0000, 2002.0000 and 1995.0000 against a limit of 6000.0000. What does the engine return?
options: A PortfolioInputError, since two projects whose capex together pass the limit cannot be entered in one inventory.
A + C at capex 5995.0000 for 780.0000, solved exactly, with overLimit false and overLimitBy 0.0000.
A + B at capex 6002.0000 for 800.0000, flagged with overLimit true and overLimitBy 2.0000 for the reader to correct.
B + C at capex 3997.0000 for 580.0000, since the engine drops the largest project whenever a pair would breach the limit.
explanation: The exact solve never exceeds the limit: A + B would cost 6002.0000, so the best set that fits is A + C at 500.0000 plus 280.0000. overLimit and overLimitBy stay in every result and read false and 0.0000 on an exact solve.

prompt: A board asks what the runner-up set at OKONO's 450.0000 limit was worth and why OK-2 dropped out. What can the engine's output answer?
options: Neither question, since the output holds the funded set, its capex and its risked EMV and names no set that came close.
Both, since the engine reports the ranked list by risked EMV per million USD beside the optimum, with 287.7500 as the best set it rejected.
The runner-up's value only, read as the gap between the set's emv of 291.0000 and its P10 high case.
The reason only, since each excluded project carries a note saying why it was left out.
explanation: The engine funds OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 for 291.0000 and says nothing about near misses; a ranked table giving 287.7500 is built by hand beside it.

prompt: Sorting OKONO by risked EMV per million USD and funding down the list at 450.0000 gives OK-1 + OK-4 + OK-5 for 287.7500. Why does the engine reach 291.0000?
options: It ranks by plain risked EMV and ignores the ratio, which puts the exploration well ahead of the workovers.
It risks each project again in the simulation, which marks down the workovers' certain success.
It compares combinations of whole projects, while a list judges projects one at a time and stops when the next one does not fit.
It uses a coarser grid than the hand list, and rounding lets the well's capex fit beside OK-1 and OK-4.
explanation: OKONO is solved exactly, solveMethod "exact" with optimalityGap 0.0000; the gain of 3.2500 comes from choosing the set, with no rounding or risk involved.

prompt: A board paper labels OK-1's capex of 120.0000 million USD with a P90. What is wrong with that label?
options: Nothing, as long as the label follows the exceedance convention, so that P90 names the capex figure the project exceeds nine times in ten.
The label is reversed, since on a cost P10 is the low figure and P90 the high figure of spending.
The label belongs to the set, so the paper should quote the 450.0000 set's P90 instead.
A capex is an amount chosen or estimated and never takes a P-label; the engine's P90 is a portfolio NPV outcome, the low case.
explanation: P-labels sit only on a simulated portfolio NPV: for the 450.0000 set P90 is -18.3574, while a capex of 120.0000 or a limit of 450.0000 carries none.

prompt: An analyst types OK-3's npv_p50 as 41.2500, its already risked value, and keeps pos 0.250000 and fail_cost 85.0000 beside it. What happens to the well?
options: Nothing changes, because the engine notices a success case smaller than the weighted fail cost and reads the entry as a value already risked.
It is risked twice, and the discounted row drops out of every budget it was funded in.
The engine sets pos to 1 for that row, since a risked npv_p50 already carries its chance and the default is applied to the weight instead.
It is funded more often, because a smaller npv_p50 narrows the success spread and the risk summary of any set holding it improves.
explanation: Weighted again by 0.250000 and still charged 0.750000 x 85.0000, the row goes below zero, and a risked EMV of 0 or less is never funded; the real 41.2500 comes from a success case of 420.0000.

prompt: An exploration well is entered with an npv_p50 and a fail_cost, but the pos field is left out of the row entirely. How does the engine value it?
options: It refuses the row, since a project with no chance of success cannot be risked and the engine names the offending project in its error.
At the middle of the range, since a missing chance of success is read as a coin toss until a value between 0 and 1 is entered.
At its npv_p50 weighted by the average pos of the other projects, which is how the engine fills a chance nobody entered.
As a certain success worth its npv_p50, since an absent pos defaults to 1.
explanation: The published unrisked case enters no pos and no fail_cost and returns 250.0000, its whole npv_p50 of 250, so a well entered with no pos is counted as if it cannot fail. A pos typed as a blank is refused by name.

prompt: OK-3's loss of 85.0000 million USD is typed with a minus sign in front, because a loss feels negative. What risked EMV does the engine return?
options: The success branch alone, because a fail_cost below 0 is read as 0 and the dry hole becomes free.
The same 41.2500, because the formula already subtracts the fail cost and the engine takes its absolute value before weighting it.
More than the success branch, since minus a negative fail cost adds the loss back as a gain.
No value, since fail_cost must be 0 or more and the engine refuses it like a negative capex.
explanation: The published negativeFailCostIsZero case, pos 0.5, npv_p50 80 and fail_cost -30, returns 40.0000, which is 0.5 x 80 with no failure branch and no warning.

prompt: The published missingNpvIsZero case enters no npv_p50, a fail_cost of 8 and a pos of 0.25, and the engine returns -6.0000. What produced that number?
options: The fail cost weighted by pos, since a row with no success case is charged its loss at its chance of success where its chance of failure belongs.
A default of 1 for the missing npv_p50, applied the way a missing pos defaults to 1.
The failure branch alone: a missing npv_p50 is 0, so 0.25 x 0 - (1 - 0.25) x 8 leaves only the loss.
The capex of 10 weighted by the chance of failure, standing in for the loss.
explanation: Every unit of -6.0000 is the failure branch: (1 - 0.25) x 8. The engine never links fail_cost to capex and never refuses a row with no NPV.

prompt: OK-3 has OKONO's largest success-case NPV, 420.0000 million USD, yet its risked EMV of 41.2500 ranks fifth of six. What takes the value away?
options: Three chances in four of a dry hole losing 85.0000, a branch that removes more than half of what the one in four success adds.
Its capex of 90.0000, which the engine subtracts from the success case before weighting what is left by the chance of success on the well.
Its wide success spread of 191.1747, charged against the success case as a penalty for uncertainty.
Its npv_p90 of 210.0000, which the engine uses as the success value when pos is below one half.
explanation: 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500, which is 0.098214 of the success case; capex and the percentiles never enter the line.

prompt: At OKONO's 450.0000 limit the funded set shows a total success NPV of 725.0000, and at 600.0000 one of 473.0000. Which reading is right?
options: The 450.0000 set is worth more, since success NPV counts every project at its npv_p50 and that is a set's value.
The 600.0000 set is worth more, 402.7500 of risked EMV against 291.0000; the larger success total comes from holding the exploration well.
The optimizer maximises success NPV at 450.0000 and risked EMV at 600.0000, where the budget can carry risk.
The two sets are worth the same, since success NPV and risked EMV converge once 10000 iterations are simulated.
explanation: Success NPV adds every best case as if all worked at once, and 725.0000 includes OK-3's 420.0000 which happens one time in four; the optimizer maximises risked EMV only.

prompt: The risk summary for OKONO's 600.0000 set reads emv 402.7500 at a correlation of 0.000000. What does emv read at a correlation of 1.000000?
options: Less than 402.7500, since projects that fail together drag the expected value down as well as widening the range of outcomes.
More than 402.7500, since projects that succeed together compound their success cases in the same draws of the simulation.
A value that depends on the seed, since emv is read from the simulated draws.
402.7500 again, since emv is the sum of the four risked EMVs and correlation changes only the spread.
explanation: 89.7500 + 115.0000 + 160.0000 + 38.0000 = 402.7500; emv comes in closed form, and correlation moves how far outcomes spread around that mean while the mean stays put.

prompt: Two projects share capex, pos, npv_p50 and fail_cost, but one has an entered success range twice as wide as the other. How does the optimizer see them?
options: It prefers the narrower one, since the knapsack penalises spread and a riskier project needs more EMV.
It prefers the wider one, since a wider range lifts npv_p10 and the engine averages it into the success case.
As identical, since the success spread feeds only the risk summary and never the risked EMV the optimizer maximises.
It cannot compare them until each has an npv_stddev, which the optimizer needs to rank projects.
explanation: The line is pos x npv_p50 - (1 - pos) x fail_cost; the spread, such as (200 - 50) / 2.5631 = 58.5229, is used only when the engine describes risk.

prompt: What does OK-3's risked EMV of 41.2500 million USD describe?
options: The most likely single result of drilling the well, since it lies between the success case and the loss.
The NPV the well delivers in a typical case, its success case moved down by the chance of success.
The median of the well's simulated outcomes, read at seed 20260829 over 10000 iterations.
An average over many such bets; in any one outcome the well succeeds around 420.0000 or fails and loses 85.0000.
explanation: No single outcome is 41.2500, and with a pos of 0.250000 the likeliest result is the loss; a set of a few risked projects can sit far from its EMV, as the 450.0000 set's P(loss) of 0.123600 shows.

prompt: A hand check writes OK-3's value as pos x npv_p50 - fail_cost. What has it done wrong?
options: Nothing, since the engine also charges the whole fail cost and weights only the success case.
Charged the full loss as if failure were certain, dropping the 0.750000 weight on the failure branch.
Counted the capex twice, since a fail cost already includes the capital spent and subtracting it again takes the capex off a second time.
Dropped the success weight, since the correct line multiplies the difference between npv_p50 and fail_cost by pos as a single term.
explanation: The hand line gives 20.0000, while 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500 is the engine value; a hand line that misses 41.2500 has dropped or doubled a weight.

prompt: A project is entered with npv_p10 50 and npv_p90 200, the wrong way round, and no npv_stddev. What does the engine do with it?
options: Returns a success spread of 0.0000, silently removing the success range from the risk summary.
Refuses the project, since an npv_p10 below npv_p90 breaks the exceedance convention.
Swaps them, since (npv_p10 - npv_p90) / 2.5631 is taken as an absolute value and gives the same 58.5229 whichever way they are typed.
Uses the negative spread, which widens the simulated range exactly as far as percentiles entered in the right order would have done.
explanation: The published invertedPercentiles case returns 0.0000 where the correct order gives 58.5229; there is no check that npv_p10 sits above npv_p90 and no message.

prompt: The published zeroStddevFallsBack case enters npv_stddev 0 with npv_p10 200 and npv_p90 50, and the success spread comes back 58.5229. Why not 0?
options: The engine holds npv_stddev at a floor of 58.5229, so that no project is ever simulated with a success spread narrower than that.
An entered standard deviation is always ignored when percentiles are present, which is why explicitStddev also returns 58.5229.
Only a positive entered standard deviation wins; a zero falls back to (200 - 50) / 2.5631.
A zero is read as missing, and a missing field takes the default of 1, which the engine then scales up by the percentile range.
explanation: explicitStddev, with npv_stddev 40, returns 40.0000, so an entered value does win when it is positive; 0 is passed over and the percentile fallback gives 58.5229.

prompt: An appraisal well's row is saved with no pos field at all, and the optimizer values it at the default of 1. Where else does that default reach?
options: Nothing else, because the risk summary draws its own success rate from the entered percentiles and only the risked EMV line uses the default.
The seeded risk summary draws it as a success in every iteration, so its funded set looks safer as well as more valuable.
The seed, because the engine reseeds the simulation whenever a default fires, recording the correction.
The optimizer's method, because a defaulted row sends the solve to the fallback grid so it can be marked.
explanation: nullPosIsDefault returns 80.0000, a certain success, and at seed 20260829 over 10000 iterations such a project never contributes a failure to P(loss) or to the P90 low case. A pos typed as 1.4 is refused before anything runs.

prompt: OK-3's success spread is 191.1747 and its mixture standard deviation 238.6507, while OK-5 reads 12.8750 on both. Why do OK-5's two figures agree?
options: The mixture also counts the drop from a success to a loss, and OK-5 cannot fail, so it has no such drop.
OK-5's percentiles are narrow, and the mixture scales the spread by the ratio of npv_p10 to npv_p90, which is close to one for the workovers.
The mixture adds capex to the spread when pos is below 1, and OK-5's pos of 1.000000 adds nothing.
The mixture is simulated, and a certain success converges so fast that the two figures meet.
explanation: OK-3 drops from a success case of 420.0000 to a loss of 85.0000, which widens 191.1747 to 238.6507; OK-5 has pos 1.000000 and a fail cost of 0.0000.

prompt: The published posZero case enters pos 0 on npv_p50 80 and fail_cost 30, and returns -30.0000. What does that value describe?
options: A pos typed below the range and read as 0, since the engine holds every chance of success between 0 and 1.
The default of 1 applied to a pos it could not read, with the success branch then charged at the fail cost.
The absolute value of the fail cost taken as a gain, since a chance of 0 reverses the sign of the failure branch.
A certain failure worth -30.0000, minus its fail cost, since a pos of 0 is inside the range the engine accepts.
explanation: -(1 - 0) x 30 = -30.0000. A pos below 0 is refused: posBelowZeroRefused gives Project "a" has a pos outside 0 to 1 (-0.2); pos must be a number from 0 to 1.

prompt: At a limit of 750.0000 million USD the engine funds OK-1 + OK-2 + OK-3 + OK-4 + OK-5 for capex 690.0000. Why is the rest of the limit left unspent?
options: The optimizer holds back a reserve against the loss probability, sized from the simulated spread of the set it has just funded.
OK-6's risked EMV per million USD is the lowest left, and the optimizer stops at the first project whose ratio falls under its cut-off.
The grid is coarse at that limit and rounds each capex up, so the five projects fill every cell although their capex sums to 690.0000.
The only project left, OK-6, costs 310.0000, and the optimizer cannot fund part of a project.
explanation: 750.0000 - 690.0000 = 60.0000 is left, and OK-6 needs 310.0000; the knapsack is solved exactly, so nothing was rounded.

prompt: A spreadsheet takes OKONO's 60.0000 left over at 750.0000, funds a matching slice of OK-6 with it, and reports a higher total than 444.0000. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since the optimizer would reach that total on a finer grid and 444.0000 is a rounding.
It describes a portfolio that cannot be built, since a slice of a tie-back delivers no share of its NPV.
The slice should be priced at OK-6's ratio of 0.464516, which the spreadsheet overstated.
The slice leaves out OK-6's fail cost of 120.0000, which has to be charged in full against any fraction of the project that is funded.
explanation: Projects are funded whole or not at all, so 444.0000 is the best buildable answer at 750.0000; OK-6 comes in only when the limit reaches 1000.0000.

prompt: Walking OKONO's ranking by risked EMV per million USD at a limit of 450.0000, funding each project that still fits, which project is the first to be skipped?
options: OK-5, whose ratio of 0.633333 falls below the cut-off once OK-4 is funded and more than half of the limit has been committed.
OK-3, whose capex of 90.0000 is skipped straight after OK-1 because the exploration well ranks last on the ratio list.

The free project's price, one million USD, which is its true cost once its capex is read at the higher limit.

That the free project was funded only where money remained after A, which a limit of 0.0000 cannot offer.
That the free project's value was checked against its cost, since the flag reads true when a set is worth less than it costs.

prompt: A user runs their own inventory and gets solveMethod "grid-feasible" with optimalityGap 200.0000. What does the gap tell them without any golden?

That the funded set may fall short of the best set that fits by at most 200.0000 of risked EMV.
That the funded capex runs 200.0000 over the limit, the amount to cut before the set is authorised.

On gridUndershootFallback it is 200.0000 and the shortfall is exactly that; on gridOvershootFallback it is 20.0000 and the shortfall is 0.0000.

The chance-weighted success case with the 85.0000 fail cost left out, because the loss is already sunk in the capex.
The success case less the fail cost, weighted by pos, which charges the 85.0000 only in the case the well works.
41.2500 risked, 0.098214 of its success-case NPV.

prompt: Step one of the method compares a hand-risked EMV with the explorer's column, and a row disagrees. What does the method say a mismatch means?

The explorer discounts the fail cost over the project life, which a hand calculation in one line cannot reproduce.
The grid rounded the project's value to a whole cell, and the hand value is the unrounded figure.
explanation: Risked EMV is closed form, pos x npv_p50 - (1 - pos) x fail_cost. nullPosIsDefault returns 80.0000 and negativeFailCostIsZero 40.0000; a pos over 1 is refused by project name and never reaches the column.

prompt: Ranked by risked EMV per million USD, OK-3 comes last at 0.458333, yet the optimizer funds it at 450.0000. Why?

The optimizer funds the cheapest projects first, and OK-3's 90.0000 is the lowest capex left after OK-5.

prompt: OKONO is solved exactly at every limit. On an inventory whose result reads solveMethod "grid-feasible", which checks does the method require even when overLimit reads false?

Cutting OK-2 reaches 291.0000 exactly, because the smaller optimum is always a subset of the larger one.
Adding OK-5 reaches 329.0000 against 402.7500, and cutting OK-2 reaches 287.7500 against 291.0000; both fall short.

options: The figure is counted from a seeded Monte Carlo, seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations here, and the seed and count are what make it reproducible.
They record the normal approximation's inputs, from which P(loss) is computed in closed form like risked EMV.
They identify the grid the optimizer solved on, which decides the funded set whose risk is being reported.
They are how the engine turns a probability into a percentile, so that 0.123600 can be quoted as the programme's P90.

prompt: OKONO's 450.0000 set shows a P90 of -18.3574 million USD. What does that number say?
options: There are nine chances in ten that the programme loses 18.3574, since the label names the probability of the loss it prints.

A cost overrun of 18.3574 on the funded capex in the low case, since the simulation draws spending as well as value.
The low case of simulated portfolio NPV is a loss, which fits a P(loss) of 0.123600.

prompt: One inventory has a row with a capex of -150, and another has a row with a negative risked EMV. What does the engine do with each?

4300000, the larger of its budget and its actual plus commitment.

Progress was re-entered between the two reports, which moves SPI but not CPI because CPI ignores progress.
Earned value and actuals do not depend on the date; planned value comes from the calendar, so SPI changes with the as-of date.
SPI is read from the S-curve, whose forecast jumps after the as-of date, while CPI is read from the budget and the actuals, which no date can change.

The work running behind schedule by that amount, since a Planned point below budget means progress fell short.

prompt: A report states only 'SPI 0.872063' and 'funded set worth 291.0000'. What is missing from each figure?
options: Its seed and iterations, as though both were simulated.

Its sign convention, since SPI and risked EMV both invert when the reporting currency changes.
Its basis: the as-of date 2027-08-15 for the SPI and the limit 450.0000 for the funded set.

That the set is the optimum, since a proof by hand covers only the three funded projects and says nothing about the three left out of the set.
That the frontier's last point matches the funded set, which only the Monte Carlo can confirm.
That the solve was exact, since solveMethod can read "exact" while a capex typed with decimals is rounded.

prompt: OK-3 is out of the OKONO set at 300.0000, in at 450.0000, out at 600.0000 and back at 750.0000. What does that path show?
options: OK-3 is marginal at 0.458333 per million USD, so the optimizer rotates it in and out of the funded set to spread the exploration risk across budgets.
Each budget is solved afresh over the whole inventory, so a project's place in one funded set promises nothing at another limit.

prompt: LOG-04 on OFON-1 carries an actual of 350000 and a commitment of 900000 against a budget of 2100000. Which of the AFE's readings does that 900000 enter?

Earned value, because a contracted order is work the line has secured, and the engine credits committed money at the line's progress percent.

The S-curve's Actual line, which adds each line's commitment on the as-of date so that the curve and the forecast read the same money.

They do not combine: SPI divides earned value by actuals to date, and time progress decides only whether the SPI is shown on the report or printed as null.

It silently clamps the figure to 100 percent on the way in, so DRL-01 earns exactly its 14200000 budget and no reading can pass what the line was authorised to cost.

The forecast is replaced by the larger of budget and actual + commitment and the line is flagged forecastIgnored "negative"; the progress stops the calculation with a message naming the cost item.
The forecast is refused with a message, since a negative cost cannot be forecast, while the progress is clamped to zero so earned value can still be summed.

CMT-03 still forecasts 1400000, so the EAC stays at 27600000, while CPI falls and percent spent rises; the S-curve does not move.

CMT-03 forecasts its budget of 1250000 again, because an entered forecast below the money already spent is read as not positive.

prompt: What is the earliest as-of date on which OFON-1 reports an SPI that is not null?
options: The day after 2027-02-01, the first date on which a whole day of the window has elapsed.

2027-02-01 itself, since the window is open on its start day and the plan begins to accrue from that morning.
2027-02-20, the date of the first invoice, since planned value waits for spend to begin before it accrues.

prompt: DRL-01 has earned 10224000 for 9800000 spent, yet its line variance reads 0. Why can its cost performance never show as a positive line variance under the forecast rule?

prompt: Suppose editing had copied every OFON-1 line's budget into its forecast field. What would the AFE report?
options: An EAC of 27600000 still, since three lines already forecast their budgets and the rule keeps the larger figure on the other two lines.
An EAC equal to the budget on the dashboard, while the S-curve keeps projecting 27600000 because the curve never reads the forecast field.
An EAC equal to the budget of 27050000 and a variance of 0: CSG-02's spent overrun and CMT-03's entered 1400000 are both overwritten, and the projected Forecast lies on the Planned line.
A variance of -150000, because CMT-03's entered forecast is protected from the copy and only CSG-02's forecast field is overwritten.

prompt: A partner's summary shows OFON-1's variance at completion as a positive 550000 and calls the AFE under budget. What should a reader check first?
options: Whether commitments were netted out, since the engine's -550000 counts the 5000000 committed, and removing them turns the variance positive.
Which way round it was taken: the engine prints budget minus forecast, so -550000 is an overrun, and a report taking forecast minus budget shows the same overrun as positive.
Whether the summary used the as-of date, since the variance at completion moves with the report date, reads positive early in the window and turns negative only once the plan passes the spend.
Whether CPI was applied, since a CPI of 1.009377 above 1 converts the rule's forecast into a saving at completion of about the same size.
explanation: 27050000 less 27600000 is -550000: the AFE expects to spend more than it was authorised, whatever sign a flipped report prints.

prompt: Two reports both print time progress 1.000000: one on an AFE run after its end date, one on an AFE saved with no window. What in the engine's metrics tells them apart?
options: The SPI, which is null on an AFE with no window because the engine cannot build a plan without dates to spread it over.
The planned value, which is 0 on an AFE with no window and the whole budget on one whose end date has passed.
Nothing: both divide earned value by the whole budget, so each SPI is percent complete over 100, and only the window fields show which AFE never had dates.
A refusal, since the engine rejects any as-of date on an AFE with no window, printing "asOf is not a valid date".
explanation: The published no-dates case returns time progress 1.000000 and SPI 0.250000, the published window read after its end returns 1.000000 and 0.940000; the Suite labels SPI unavailable when there are no dates.

prompt: The published "suite test: empty AFE: no budget and no spend, so SPI and CPI are null" returns SPI null, and OFON-1 as of 2027-01-15 returns SPI null too. What separates the two nulls?

A new invoice, because after the end of the window SPI is computed from the S-curve's Actual line in place of the typed progress.
Only progress entered on the lines, because planned value has stopped at the approved budget and a later date or a revised EAC cannot move it.

prompt: LOG-04 places a further order large enough that its actual + commitment passes its 2100000 budget, and nothing is invoiced or paid. Which readings move?

Nothing until the order is invoiced, since commitments enter the forecast only when an invoice ties them to a line.

The engine applies the CPI of 1.009377 to the calendar fraction before printing it, which lifts time progress above the ratio that the Planned line gives.

prompt: A drilling superintendent asks which OFON-1 line the SPI of 0.872063 as of 2027-08-15 says is running late. What can the SPI answer?

CMP-05, since a line at 0.0000 percent is the only one that puts nothing into earned value while its whole budget sits in the plan.
DRL-01, since the largest line carries most of the planned value and so alone decides whether the AFE reads below 1.
Every line whose progress is under 0.645695 of its work, since SPI sets each line's progress against the window's time progress.

prompt: The published window from 2020-01-01 to 2020-12-31, read as of 2020-06-30, has one line with a budget of 1200, an actual of 200, a commitment of 100 and an entered forecast of 1500. What is the line's EAC, and where does it appear on the curve?

prompt: Presenting OFON-1's S-curve, a cost engineer explains the rise in Forecast from 15090000 at Aug 27 to 19374834 at Sep 27 as the commitments falling due in September. What does produce the rise?

The remaining budget projected at the AFE's CPI of 1.009377 from the last actual of 15090000, which the curve adds on month by month until it reaches the end of the window.
A spending surge expected in September from DRL-01's remaining budget, which the forecast rule schedules into the first month after the report's date because drilling is the largest line.

prompt: A new AFE is reported as of its start day. Progress is typed on its budgeted lines but no actuals have been entered. What CPI and SPI does the engine print?

prompt: A published S-curve on a window from 2090-01-01 to 2091-01-01 has three lines: budget 1200 with actual 900 and commitment 600; budget 500 with forecast 650; budget 300 with forecast -10. Its last Forecast point is 2450. Which reading of the lines produces that figure?

prompt: A group capital summary adds OFON-1's operator share of 6762500 to the risked EMV of 402.7500 on OKONO's 600.0000 set. What is wrong with the sum?

Only the timing: the operator's share should be taken on the EAC of 27600000 in place of the budget, so that both figures describe the end of the programme and can be summed.
Nothing, since an operator's share and a risked EMV are both the operator's expected outlay, and they add directly.

prompt: OFON-1's operator carries 25.0000 percent. A statement of costs incurred to date bills the operator 6762500. What went wrong?
options: Nothing, because a working interest is always billed on the authorised amount, and actual spend settles only when the AFE is closed.
It billed the operator's share of the 27050000 budget; the share of the 15090000 actually spent is 3772500.
It billed on the EAC of 27600000, which carries the forecast overrun, where a statement of costs to date should bill the budget.
It billed the operator on actuals plus the 5000000 committed, which a statement of costs to date leaves out until the orders are paid.

prompt: Seeing 10224000 earned for 9800000 spent, DRL-01's cost engineer enters a forecast between its 12400000 of actual + commitment and its 14200000 budget. What changes?
options: DRL-01 forecasts the entered figure, so the EAC and the projected Forecast fall and the line shows a saving the fallback could never show; CPI, SPI and earned value stay.
Nothing, because the rule keeps the larger of an entered figure and the budget, so the line still forecasts 14200000.
The EAC falls and CPI rises with it, since an entered forecast under the budget is read as cost performance on the line.
Nothing yet, since an entry under the budget on an unfinished line is treated as not positive until the line reaches 100.0000 percent.
