prompt: CSG-02 enters OFON-1's EAC at 4300000 and its earned value at 3900000. Which figure is the engine's error?
options: The earned value, because a line that is 100.0000 percent complete should earn what it actually cost, so the 4300000 spent on casing belongs in both of the readings.
The EAC, because a finished line should forecast its budget of 3900000 once its typed progress reaches 100.0000 percent, and the extra spend belongs in the variance alone.
Both, because the two readings should agree on a finished line, and the gap of 400000 between them shows a commitment counted twice after its order was paid.
Neither: the forecast rule takes actual + commitment because it passes the budget, while earned value is budget times progress and never reads the actual.
explanation: Earned value pays each line what its work was authorised to cost, 3900000, which is exactly what lets it be set against the 4300000 spent; the rule forecasts what the line has cost.

prompt: An AFE whose window spans today is opened on two days in a row with nothing changed on its lines, and the as-of box is left at its default each time. What differs between the two openings?
options: The EAC, because the forecast rule reads the as-of date to decide which invoices count toward each cost line.
The CPI, because actuals are pro-rated to the as-of date across the window before they are divided into earned value.
The SPI, because the dashboard passes today as the as-of date by default; OFON-1 run for 2027-08-15 gives planned value 17466060 on any day.
Nothing, since the engine reads the window's end date for every calculation and the as-of date only labels the report.
explanation: The engine never reads the clock: every call states its as-of date, and only time progress, planned value and SPI move with it. The dashboard supplies today unless a date is typed into its As of box.

prompt: CMP-05 has 1200000 committed, nothing spent and progress of 0.0000. What does the line put into OFON-1's readings?
options: Its 1200000 commitment into percent spent and its budget into earned value, since a line with orders placed is counted as started.
Nothing into any reading, since a line at 0.0000 percent is left out of the AFE's totals until its work begins.
Nothing into earned value or percent spent, its 5600000 budget into the EAC, and the same budget into the plan that SPI divides by, which pulls SPI down.
Its commitment into the EAC in place of its budget, because a committed line forecasts the money promised on it.
explanation: The fallback takes the larger of 5600000 and 1200000, and planned value of 17466060 is spread over all 27050000 of budget, including completion work that has not begun.

prompt: On OFON-1 as of 2027-08-15, suppose a line's typed actual already includes an amount whose invoice is dated in September. Where does that money appear?
options: In both, since the curve reads the line actuals up to the as-of date and switches to the invoices only after it.
In neither, since the engine holds a line's actual back until the date of the invoice that supports it has been reached.
On the curve only, which plots the invoice at Sep 27 as a projected actual, while the line's actual waits for the next report.
In percent spent and CPI, which read the line, and on no point of the Actual line, which is null past the as-of date.
explanation: The metrics read the line column and the curve the invoices, and the curve cuts an invoice dated after the as-of date; at Sep 27 its Actual is null while CPI still reads 1.009377.

prompt: OFON-1's window is saved with its start date a month late by mistake, and nothing else changes. Which readings does the error reach?
options: Every reading, because earned value is pro-rated across the window and CPI then divides that pro-rated figure by the actuals.
Time progress, planned value, SPI and the S-curve's points and Planned line; the EAC, earned value, CPI, percent spent and percent complete are read from the lines and stay.
Only the S-curve, because SPI takes its planned value from the budget and the as-of date, and never from the window.
The EAC as well as SPI, because the forecast rule falls back to the budget only on lines whose window has already opened.
explanation: Planned value is the budget times the elapsed fraction of the window, 0.645695 of 27050000 at 2027-08-15 on the true dates, so only the calendar readings follow a wrong start.

prompt: Drawn as of 2027-06-30, earlier than the usual 2027-08-15, how many points does OFON-1's S-curve carry, and why?

One more, since a report dated inside the window adds a point on the as-of date so that the plan behind the SPI can be read.
As many as the months to the present, since the walk runs on from the start date to the current calendar month.

A schedule ratio that has fallen because the plan kept growing after the end date while earned value stood still on the lines.
The first reading corrected for the 256 of 729 days, applied once the window closed to turn a mid-window ratio into a final one.
The case's CPI, which the engine substitutes for SPI once the window has closed and planned value cannot be computed any more.

prompt: CMT-03's engineer clears the entered forecast of 1400000, leaving the field blank. What happens to the line and to OFON-1?

CMT-03 falls back to its budget of 1250000, the larger against 940000, so the variance at completion shrinks to CSG-02's -400000 and the projected Forecast is drawn lower.
Nothing, since a blank field keeps the last positive forecast the line held, and the EAC stays at 27600000.
CMT-03 forecasts 0 and the variance at completion turns positive, because a blank forecast is read as a descope.
explanation: CMT-03's -150000 existed only because it was typed; the spend overrun on CSG-02, -400000, stays because it rests on money already spent.

options: An entered forecast smaller than the money already spent and committed on the line, which the rule declines to take.
An invoice whose date is null, which the curve refuses outright and so leaves out of every bucket it draws.
A progress figure below zero on a cost line, refused with a message that names the item.
An entered forecast below zero, which the message says lies outside what a line can cost.

No, because the EAC is never below actual + commitment, so no share of it can fall under the invoices at any point.
Only when an entered forecast is negative, since the S-curve takes a negative entry at its face value and pulls the projected line down under the actuals.
Yes: the projection never starts from the actuals, so an AFE whose invoices ran ahead of a straight spread of its EAC would step down at the as-of date.

That it is likely to hold, since a CPI of 1.009377 above 1 shows the lines buying work under budget, which caps any further overrun.
That it is unlikely to grow, since the rule already forecasts every line at the larger of its budget and its actual + commitment.
That it is likely on the drilling line, since DRL-01 at 72.0000 percent complete has the least work left in which to overrun.

prompt: OFON-1's Actual line sits above its Planned line at Mar 27, below it at Apr 27, above at May 27 and below at Jun 27. What do those swings say about the well?
options: That cost performance swung above and below 1 each month, since each crossing marks CPI passing through parity on the lines.
Nothing: invoices arrive in lumps and the plan is a straight line in days, so each crossing is an invoice date meeting that line.
That the schedule alternated between ahead and behind, because the Actual line is the earned value the SPI divides by.
That drilling was front-loaded and then paused, which the engine's plan reflects by phasing DRL-01's budget into the early months of the window.

prompt: OFON-1 is authorised at 27050000 USD and the engine forecasts 27600000 on the same lines. Which lines lift the forecast past the authorisation, and by what figure on each?
options: DRL-01 and CMP-05, the two largest budgets, because a forecast at completion grows with the size of the lines it adds and those two carry most of the AFE.
LOG-04 and CMP-05, whose commitments of 900000 and 1200000 are added on top of their budgets once a contractor order has been placed against the line.
CSG-02, which has already spent 4300000 against a budget of 3900000, and CMT-03, whose entered forecast of 1400000 stands over its budget of 1250000.
DRL-01 and CSG-02, the two lines that have spent most of their budgets, since the forecast projects each line's spend forward at its current rate.

prompt: A cost report prints LOG-04 as 350000 spent of a 2100000 budget, a line that looks barely touched. What has the report left out?
options: The 900000 committed to contractors and not yet paid, so 1250000 of the line is already spoken for.
The invoices billed against the line, which would lift its actual to the 4400000 dated 2027-06-05 once they are posted to it.
Its entered forecast, which the engine substitutes for the budget on every line that has spent less than half of its authorisation.
Its progress of 20.0000 percent, which turns the 350000 spent into 420000 of work and shows the line running ahead of its budget.

prompt: A contractor order on DRL-01 is paid and its amount is moved into the line's actual, but nobody takes it out of the commitment. What happens?
options: The engine matches the paid amount against the commitment it came from and removes it, so the line's forecast is unchanged by the move.
The engine refuses the line once actual plus commitment passes the budget, and its message names the cost item carrying the excess.
Nothing moves in any reading, because the forecast rule reads the budget and the entered forecast and never looks at the commitment column.
Actual plus commitment counts the order twice, and the forecast rule can read the double count as an overrun without any check.
explanation: The commitment is a typed figure the engine never ties to a contract or an invoice; DRL-01 already carries 9800000 spent and 2600000 committed, 12400000, against 14200000.

prompt: OFON-1 reads 55.7856 percent spent. What sits in the numerator of that figure?
options: Actuals and commitments together, because money promised to a contractor is money the AFE cannot spend on anything else.
Only the 15090000 of actuals on the lines; the 5000000 committed stays outside it.
The earned value of 15231500, since percent spent measures how much of the authorised budget the finished work has used up.
The invoice total, because a spend percentage is a reading of money that has left the company and only the invoices carry a date.
explanation: Percent spent is 15090000 over the budget of 27050000. CPI and percent spent read the line actuals only; commitments enter the forecast rule and nothing else.

prompt: A fifth invoice is entered on OFON-1 and no line's actual is changed. Which reading moves?
options: CPI and percent spent, which read spend, while the curve reads line actuals.
The S-curve's Actual series, while CPI, percent spent and the EAC stay where they were.
The EAC, on the line the engine matches to the invoice by its amount.
Every reading, since the engine reconciles invoices with line actuals.
explanation: The metrics read actuals from the cost lines and the S-curve reads the dated invoices; OFON-1's four invoices and its line actuals both total 15090000 only by construction.

prompt: An invoice on an AFE is saved with a null date. What does the engine do with it?
options: Refuses the AFE with an error that names the invoice, in the way negative progress on a cost line is refused.
Counts it from 1970, which is earlier than every bucket, so it appears in the S-curve from the first point on.
Places it at the as-of date, so it lifts only the points from that day onward and leaves the earlier ones alone.
Leaves it off the S-curve and reports it in the count of undated invoices beside the curve.
explanation: The engine does not refuse an undated invoice and does not guess a date for one: an invoice it cannot date reaches no bucket, and the count is reported beside the curve, 2 on the published undated case.

prompt: A reviewer sees 15090000 of actuals on the OFON-1 dashboard and 15090000 at the last Actual point of its S-curve. What has the reviewer established?
options: That two totals match, which says nothing about whether every invoice is dated or where each one's money went.
That every invoice was posted to the right line, since the curve sums invoices by cost code.
That the line actuals are correct, because the curve is built from those same line actuals and could not reach the total otherwise.
That the engine reconciled the two records, since it declines to draw a curve whose invoices disagree with the actuals on the lines.
explanation: The engine reconciles nothing: an invoice carries a date and an amount and no cost code, and on OFON-1 the 15090000 agreement holds by construction.

prompt: OFON-1 carries an invoice of 5200000 dated 2027-04-10. Which cost line is it for?
options: DRL-01, the only line whose actual of 9800000 is large enough to hold it.
Every line in proportion to its actual, as the engine spreads each invoice.
The AFE cannot say, because an invoice carries a date and an amount and no cost code.
CSG-02, since the engine books an invoice to the nearest line actual.
explanation: The line actuals say where the money went and the invoices say when; no OFON-1 invoice equals any line's actual, and the 5200000 could be drilling, casing or both.

prompt: Casing bought in another currency is to be entered on OFON-1, which is kept in USD. Where is the exchange rate held?
options: In a currency code held on each cost line, so every line converts at its own rate before the engine totals the budget of 27050000.
In the partner split, which bills each partner in its own currency.
Beside each invoice, so the S-curve can restate the casing spend in USD.
Nowhere in the AFE: the amount is converted before it is typed, at a rate the engine never sees.
explanation: The AFE holds one currency code for its lines, invoices and partners and no exchange rate among its inputs; OFON-1's 27050000 is whole USD as the engine prints it.

prompt: A cost line is typed in a local currency beside four lines kept in USD. What does the engine do with it?
options: Adds it to the other lines without complaint, because it holds one currency code and has no way to know.
Refuses the AFE, since a line whose amounts are out of scale with the rest fails the same input check that refuses negative progress.
Flags the line and leaves it out of the EAC until an exchange rate is supplied.
Converts it at the exchange rate stored with the AFE's currency code.

prompt: Why would OFON-1's CPI of 1.009377 read the same if every amount on the AFE were restated in one other currency?
options: The engine converts every amount to USD before it forms a ratio, so the currency the lines are typed in never reaches the index.
It is 15231500 over 15090000, one amount over another in the same currency, so the unit cancels.
CPI is formed from the progress percents alone, which carry no currency.
It would not, since CPI is quoted against USD and needs the rate applied.
explanation: Earned value over actuals divides like by like; percent spent 55.7856 and percent complete 56.3087 cancel the unit the same way.

prompt: Someone rewrites OFON-1's budget of 27050000 in millions, rounded, to lay it beside a capital portfolio figure in million USD. What is wrong?
options: Only the rounding, since at four decimals the budget would sit correctly in a portfolio sum.
Only the scale, since the portfolio is kept in thousands of USD and the budget has to be divided by a thousand before it is added.
The two models share nothing, and the rescaled figure is a number the engine never printed and nobody can check.
Only the sign, since the portfolio records a capex as a negative figure and the budget has to be negated before the two are added.
explanation: OFON-1 is whole USD against line budgets and the portfolio is million USD with whole projects against a limit; a figure from one never belongs in a sum with the other.

prompt: One cost line is saved with a progress of -0.5 percent and another with progress past 100 percent. What does the engine do?
options: Refuses both, each with a message naming its cost item, since progress runs from 0 to 100 percent.
Refuses the first with a message naming the cost item, and accepts the second, letting it earn more than its budget.
Clamps both into the range, reading the first as 0 and the second as 100, and reports the clamped figures as though they were typed.
Accepts both with a flag, leaving the flagged lines out of earned value while still carrying their budgets in the EAC and the total.
explanation: Negative progress fails with "Cost item "Completion" has negative progress (-0.5 percent)." and progress above 100 fails the same way, naming the line; progress of exactly 100 is accepted and earns the whole budget.

prompt: OFON-1 is reported again on a later date with every line unchanged. Which of its four headline readings can change?
options: The EAC, since a forecast at completion is recomputed from the spend expected by the date of the report and moves with each one.
CPI, since actuals are counted only up to the as-of date of the report.
All four, since every figure the engine prints is a reading of one day.

The 15090000 spent plus the 5000000 committed plus the budgets of unstarted lines.

The rest of the budget at the line's progress rate, since the rule extrapolates a line from its progress once spend passes the budget.
Twice its spend and commitment, projected from its half-done progress.

Each line's actual times its progress, with the invoice total standing in for lines that have not reported.

prompt: CSG-02 is 100.0000 percent complete, having spent 4300000 against a budget of 3900000. What does it earn?

3900000, its budget, since earned value pays each line what its work was authorised to cost.
The larger of its budget and its actual, the same choice the forecast rule makes on a line with no forecast.

prompt: "progress of exactly 100 percent is accepted and earns the whole budget" returns earned value 140.0000 against actuals of 100.0000 and CPI 1.400000. What does that CPI record?

A clamp, since the engine caps progress at 100 percent and 1.400000 is the index it reports at that cap.
An inverted index, actuals over earned value, which the engine switches to once a line reaches 100 percent.

0.563087, since time progress falls back to 1 when no day has elapsed.

The EAC, which absorbed the overrun of -550000 between the reports and raised the plan that SPI is divided by.

195 whole days elapsed since 2027-02-01, over the 302 whole days from the start to the end of the window.
The whole months elapsed at the first of August over the months in the window, since the plan steps once a month.
The days elapsed since the first invoice on 2027-02-20 over the days to the end, since the plan starts when spending does.

Either one, because a difference of a few units on a budget of 27050000 is inside the rounding of whole-unit AFE money.
The product of the EAC and the printed fraction, because planned value is recomputed against the forecast once the AFE overruns.
13345861, because the engine multiplies the unrounded fraction.

prompt: OFON-1's SPI is above 1 at 2027-06-30 and below 1 at 2027-08-15. DRL-01's rig time, 14200000 of the budget, is spent early and CMP-05's 5600000 of completion late. What can the two SPIs be, before any slippage is assumed?
options: The shape of a well measured against a plan that is a straight line in calendar days and knows nothing about which work comes first.
Proof that the job was ahead in June and fell behind in August, since both readings divide the same earned value by a correct plan for each day.
A phasing error in the plan, since the engine front-loads DRL-01's budget and the plan overshoots the work by August.
The effect of CPI 1.009377, which scales planned value by cost performance and pulls SPI below 1 once spend outruns the plan.

prompt: Between OFON-1's reports of 2027-06-30 and 2027-08-15, SPI fell while earned value stayed at 15231500. What can the engine tell you about why?

That the rig stood idle, because SPI below 1 on the second date is the engine's measure of lost working days against the window.

prompt: As of 2028-01-10, after OFON-1's window closed on 2027-11-30, SPI is 0.563087. What does that number measure?

Earned value over the whole budget, which is percent complete 56.3087 divided by 100, so it has stopped measuring pace against a plan.

The average of the SPIs reported across the window, which the engine carries forward once no further planned value accrues.

prompt: OFON-1's planned value stops at 27050000 on and after its end day, though its EAC is 27600000. What does that mean for a late AFE that is also overrunning?

Its overrun of -550000 appears as a schedule loss, because planned value absorbs the variance at completion on the end day.
Nothing, because SPI stops being reported once the window has closed.
It is measured against the approved budget, the smaller number, because the forecast never enters planned value.

prompt: The published case with no window dates returns time progress 1.000000 and SPI 0.250000. What does the engine do with an AFE saved without a window?
options: Refuses it with AfeInputError, because planned value cannot be formed without a start date and an end date.
Reports SPI null, as it does before the start, because with no window no day has elapsed inside it.
Reports it as though the window had already ended, dividing earned value by the whole budget, and the Suite labels its SPI unavailable.
Measures it against today, treating the report date as the end of the window so that time progress is always 1 on the day it runs.

prompt: An as-of date of 30 February is passed to an AFE that has no window dates at all. What does the engine return?
options: A refusal, AfeInputError: "asOf is not a valid date", even though the AFE has no window the date could be placed in.
Time progress 1.000000 and the no-dates SPI, because without a window the as-of date is never read and cannot be wrong.
A report dated the first valid day after the typed one, since the date parser rolls an impossible day forward into March.
SPI null, because an unreadable date is treated as a date before the start, where planned value is 0.

prompt: OFON-1's lines are saved on an AFE with no window dates. What SPI does a report show on the first day of drilling?
options: Null, because a report on the first day of drilling falls on the start of the window, where no whole day has elapsed.
Infinity, because the engine divides earned value by a planned value of 0 whenever it is run before the plan has grown.
1.141290, because the engine reads the clock and the first day of drilling comes early in the window, where the plan is small.
0.563087, the same as on its last day.
explanation: With no window, time progress falls back to 1, so SPI equals percent complete 56.3087 divided by 100 on whatever day the report is opened; the Suite labels it unavailable.

prompt: A monthly pack labelled as of 2027-08-15 divides OFON-1's earned value of 15231500 by a planned value of 13345861 and prints 1.141290. What went wrong?
options: Nothing, because earned value and CPI are the same on both dates, so SPI is too and the pack simply chose the more favourable planned value.
The earned value is stale, because earned value as of 2027-08-15 is larger than in June and the numerator should have been updated with it.
The planned value belongs to 2027-06-30, so the pack reports June's SPI under August's date; as of 2027-08-15 planned value is 17466060 and SPI 0.872063.
The pack used planned value where it should have used actuals of 15090000, which is the August denominator the engine divides by.
explanation: Dividing an earned value from one date by a planned value from another is the second form of the undated SPI; the engine's planned value for 2027-08-15 is 17466060.

prompt: A report dated 2027-01-15, before OFON-1's window opens, shows earned value 15231500 from DRL-01 at 72.0000 percent and CSG-02 at 100.0000 percent. What does the engine make of that?
options: It sets earned value to 0 before the start, since work cannot be earned before a window opens, and reports CPI null beside it.
It reports it without complaint, since it never asks whether progress is plausible for the date, so the reader must suspect the window or the progress column.
It flags the AFE invalid, since earned value above a planned value of 0 is a combination the engine refuses to report.
It reports SPI null and zeroes the progress it cannot schedule, leaving only CSG-02's finished line in earned value.
explanation: Before the start SPI is null, but earned value 15231500, CPI 1.009377 and the EAC of 27600000 are all still reported, because they are read from the lines and the calendar plays no part in them.

prompt: OFON-1's S-curve as of 2027-08-15 opens on a point labelled "Feb 27". What does that label denote?
options: The 27th of February, the monthly billing cut-off to which each point's invoices are summed.
The last day of February 2027, since each point closes its month and carries that month's invoices.
February 2027, a short month name and a two-digit year, on a point standing on the start date 2027-02-01 with every column cumulative to that day.
Point 27 of the window, counted in days from the start, which is where the first bucket is closed.
explanation: Each point sits on the start date stepped forward by whole months, the 1st on OFON-1, so the invoice of 2027-02-20 shows an Actual of 0 at Feb 27 and first appears at Mar 27.

prompt: A monthly report reads OFON-1's "Jul 27" Actual of 12700000 as spend to the end of July, then flags an August spike of 2390000 at "Aug 27". What happened?
options: The invoice of 2027-07-18 is dated after the 1 July point and first counts at the 1 August point, so the spike is a reading of the labels and no August spending.
The invoice was billed in July but paid in August, and the curve records invoices when they are paid.
August's point includes the commitments on the lines, which enter the Actual line once a month closes.
The curve lags spend by one bucket by design, so the August point is July's spend delayed to hold accruals out.
explanation: Actual at a point counts invoices dated on or before that day, so Jul 27 holds 3100000, 5200000 and 4400000, and 2390000 takes Aug 27 to 15090000.

prompt: OFON-1's metrics report planned value 17466060 as of 2027-08-15. Where does that number sit on the S-curve drawn at the same as-of date?
options: On the Aug 27 point, which the engine moves to the as-of date whenever the date falls inside that month, so the chart and the SPI agree.
On the Forecast line, where planned value is redrawn from the EAC.
On the Sep 27 point, because the curve rounds the as-of date forward to the next bucket so that the plan it shows is never understated.
On no point: it falls between Aug 27 at 16212086 and Sep 27 at 18988742, since no bucket stands on the as-of date.
explanation: The buckets are a fixed monthly grid with no point on the as-of date, so the planned value SPI 0.872063 was divided by is not plotted, and earned value 15231500 is not plotted at all.

prompt: OFON-1's Planned line adds 2687086 into the May 27 point but 2776656 into the Aug 27 point. Why do the steps differ?
options: The plan is phased by cost line, and DRL-01's rig time weights the drilling months more heavily than later ones.
The plan is straight in calendar days, so a month with more days adds more plan.
Each step is the budget less the invoices so far spread over the months left, so it changes as invoices arrive.
The engine rounds each point to whole units separately, and the rounding error accumulates into alternating steps.
explanation: Planned is the budget of 27050000 times elapsed days over the days in the window; the month into May 27 is shorter than the month into Aug 27, so it adds 2687086 against 2776656.

prompt: A planner wants OFON-1's Planned line to front-load DRL-01's 14200000 of rig time and hold CMP-05's 5600000 of completion to the end. What does the engine offer?
options: A phasing field on each line, which reshapes the Planned line once every line carries a start and end month of its own.
Nothing: it draws one straight line for the whole AFE, with no plan per line and no phasing to enter, charging every calendar day an equal slice of the budget.
An S-shaped plan by default, since the curve's name promises one and the straight line appears only for an AFE with a single line, which the engine bends to the invoices.
A plan per line summed across the window, which the engine builds from each line's progress so that finished work is planned early.
explanation: The plan has no shape the user can give it, so an Actual above Planned at Mar 27 and below it at Apr 27 is an invoice date meeting a straight line and not news about the well.

prompt: At OFON-1's Aug 27 point the Actual is 15090000 and the Planned is 16212086. A reader calls the gap "behind schedule". What is the gap?
options: Earned value below planned value on the day of the point, which is the curve's plot of SPI in money in place of a ratio at each of the monthly buckets it draws.
Commitments not yet invoiced, which the Actual line holds back until billing and which the Planned line already includes.
Spend below a straight budget line, a cost comparison with no progress in it; the schedule measure is SPI 0.872063, earned value over planned value.
Schedule slippage in money, since planned value and actual cost measured on the same day together form the schedule variance that the curve plots at every point.
explanation: SPI divides earned value, 15231500 from the progress column, by planned value; the curve never plots earned value, so no gap on it is a schedule reading.

prompt: On a live AFE the cost lines' actuals total more than the S-curve's last Actual at or before the as-of date. What is each describing?
options: Percent spent and CPI describe the actuals typed on the lines, the Actual line describes the dated invoices, and nothing on the screen says which is which, so the difference is a question about accruals, billing or a missing date.
The same money on two schedules, since the curve converts line actuals into invoices by date and the gap is spend not yet reached by a bucket.
An error in the engine, since it forces the invoices to match the lines and a gap can only mean the curve was drawn from stale data.
Commitments, since the lines carry actual plus commitment and the curve carries the actual alone, and the gap is what is on order.
explanation: The metrics sum the actual column and the S-curve sums invoices; on OFON-1 both read 15090000 because the teaching field was written to match, which teaches the wrong habit.

prompt: A published case bills two invoices over a past window: 100 with no date field and 200 whose date is null. The first and last points both read an Actual of 0. What happened to each invoice?
options: The null date was read as a day in 1970 and counted in every bucket of the curve, while the invoice with no date field never counted at all.
The engine refused the missing field and dropped that invoice with a warning, while it booked the null date at the start of the window as an opening balance.
Both counted on the as-of date, the only day an undated invoice can take.
Neither could be dated, so neither reached the curve, and the engine reported 2 undated invoices beside it.
explanation: An invoice the engine cannot date reaches no bucket, however its date is missing; the count of undated invoices, 2 here, is reported beside the curve so the money is named.

prompt: OFON-1's Forecast reads 15090000 at Aug 27 and 19374834 at Sep 27, the first point after the as-of date of 2027-08-15. What is the step?
options: The spend expected in September, the EAC less the actuals to date spread over the months left in the window.
A change of formula: past the as-of date the Forecast is the EAC spread from the start of the window, ignoring the actuals it follows.
The commitments of 5000000 falling due in the first month after the report, added onto the last Actual as they are billed by the contractors.
A burn rate taken from the last invoices and carried forward from 15090000, which is why the step repeats at each projected point until the end.
explanation: The projection never starts from 15090000 and adds spend still to come; the step's size depends on how far the actuals sit from a straight line, which says nothing about September.

prompt: Why does OFON-1's Forecast sit above Planned at every projected point, 19374834 against 18988742 at Sep 27 and 24949669 against 24452483 at Nov 27?
options: It scales the plan by CPI 1.009377, so every projected point is lifted by the cost performance of the work done so far.
It adds the commitments of 5000000 to the plan from the as-of date, since committed money is certain to be spent.
It is the Planned line redrawn with the EAC of 27600000 in place of the budget of 27050000.
It carries forward the gap between Actual and Planned at the last actual point, holding that gap constant to the end.
explanation: The EAC exceeds the budget by a variance at completion of -550000 and the whole projected line carries that ratio; earned value and CPI play no part in the projection.

prompt: Suppose CSG-02's budget were typed into its forecast field. What would that do to CSG-02 and to OFON-1's Forecast line?
options: The copy is a positive entered forecast, so the rule takes 3900000 whatever CSG-02 has spent, hiding its line variance of -400000 and settling the Forecast line toward the Planned line.
Nothing to CSG-02, because the rule compares an entered forecast with actual plus commitment and keeps the larger 4300000.
It would have raised CSG-02's forecast to its actual, since a copied budget is recognised as a default and ignored by the rule.
It would have removed CSG-02 from the EAC, since a forecast equal to the budget carries no variance and the line drops out.
explanation: A positive entered forecast wins under the one rule, so a typed 3900000 replaces the 4300000 already spent in the EAC; the engine flags the line forecastBelowCommitted, but the forecast stands.

prompt: OFON-1's Nov 27 point plans 24452483 against a budget of 27050000. Does the S-curve's plan stop short of the budget?
options: Yes, because the curve spreads the budget over the months before the end month and leaves the final month for contingency that is never planned.
Yes, because the engine deducts the 2597517 held for the month the as-of date falls in, and releases it once a later report is run.
No, because the curve rescales its last point to the budget when the chart is drawn, and 24452483 is only the value in the underlying table.
No. Nov 27 is only the last monthly point; the closing point "30 Nov 27" carries Planned 27050000, as the metrics do on the end day.
explanation: The walk steps from 2027-02-01 by whole months; the next step falls after 2027-11-30, so the curve closes on a point dated the end, adding the last 2597517 of plan.

prompt: A published window from 2090-01-01 to 2091-01-01 returns 13 points ending "1 Jan 91", and OFON-1 returns 11 ending "30 Nov 27". Both last points carry the whole EAC. Why is there no separate monthly point on 2091-01-01?
options: Its window lies wholly in the future, so the whole curve is projection, and the engine drops any monthly point that would only repeat the EAC already printed beside it.
Its end date falls exactly on a monthly step, so the closing point replaces that step and no date appears twice; OFON-1's end is not on a step from 2027-02-01.
It has no invoices, so no actual needs a point of its own, while OFON-1's four invoices each hold a monthly point open.
It is thirteen months long, and the engine merges the last two points of any window longer than a year so that a chart never carries more than thirteen labels.
explanation: Every curve closes on a point dated the window end with Planned the budget and Forecast the EAC. When a monthly step lands on the end, the closing point takes its place; OFON-1's steps land on the first of each month, so Nov 27 is followed by "30 Nov 27".

prompt: The course draws OFON-1's first point as "Feb 27". A viewer in America/Los_Angeles opens the same AFE. What does the curve show there?
options: The same amounts relabelled, since the Suite converts the month labels into the viewer's local calendar before drawing them.
A later as-of date, since the Planned line is recomputed from today's date in the viewer's time zone.
The same curve: the window, the as-of date, the monthly step, the day count and every label are read in UTC, so the first point is "Feb 27" there too.
A first point labelled "Jan 27" and every Planned value shifted, since the window is parsed at midnight and west of UTC that midnight falls on the previous evening.
explanation: The S-curve is read in UTC, so every zone draws what a UTC machine draws; the published February-start case labels its first point "Feb 27" in every zone, and OFON-1's Mar 27 plans 2507947 everywhere.

prompt: The published window 2020-01-01 to 2020-12-31 with two invoices returns 13 points. Where does the curve end, and what does its last point carry?
options: On the as-of date, so a window read after its end draws no point beyond the day of the report.
On the last monthly step, "Dec 20", which stands on the first of December, with Planned short of the budget of 1200 by the whole plan for December.
On the twelfth monthly point, since the engine limits every curve to twelve points whatever the window length.
On a closing point "31 Dec 20" dated the window end, with Planned 1200, the budget, and Actual 350 from the invoices to that day.
explanation: Twelve monthly points from 2020-01-01 are followed by a closing point dated the end, windowEnd true, with Planned 1200 and Forecast 1200; its Actual counts the invoices dated on or before the end, 350.

prompt: A graded reading of OFON-1 is worked with every calculation right, but the explorer was left on its default as-of date of today when the task named 2027-08-15. Which of its metric readings are wrong?
options: Every number that depends on the lines, since the explorer recomputes earned value and the EAC for the date it is set to.
Earned value, CPI and SPI, since all three divide by a figure the engine reads on the day the report is run.
None, since the dashboard passes today as the as-of date and a report run today is the current reading of the AFE.
Only time progress, planned value and SPI.
explanation: EAC 27600000, variance -550000, earned value 15231500 and CPI 1.009377 are identical at every date, so the answer looks complete while its SPI answers a different question from 0.872063.

prompt: Working OFON-1 in the order lines, forecast, earned value, date, curve, at which step does an entered forecast that is not positive first become visible?
options: The curve step, where the Forecast line jumps at the as-of date on any line whose entered forecast was ignored by the rule, lifting that line above the Planned line.
The forecast step, where the branch each line took is written, because the rule ignores that figure and the line's fallback looks ordinary in the EAC.
The earned value step, where a line with no usable forecast earns nothing on its progress and pulls CPI down.
The date step, since an entered forecast of 0 or less is treated as unplanned work and zeroes that line's planned value.
explanation: The published negative forecast case returns EAC 100.0000 and variance 0.0000 with an entered -50, a total that shows nothing, so only the named branch on the line reveals it.

prompt: OFON-1's variance at completion is -550000. DRL-01, LOG-04 and CMP-05 each show a line variance of 0. What do those three zeros say?
options: Only that spend and commitment have not yet passed the budget on those lines; with no entered forecast a line can never show a saving, so 0 is the rule's floor, and the whole -550000 is CSG-02's -400000 plus CMT-03's -150000.
That the three lines are on budget, since the rule forecasts each at the larger of budget and spend and none has gone over.
That the three lines are under budget by their unspent balances, which the rule nets against the overruns on the other two.
That the three lines are complete, since the forecast rule reports a zero variance once a line's progress reaches its budget.
explanation: DRL-01 has 12400000 spent and committed against 14200000; its forecast is still 14200000, and any overrun still to come on drilling, logging or completion is not in the -550000.

prompt: With CMT-03's budget of 1250000 and the 940000 already spent and committed, an entered forecast of 900000 gives an item forecast of 900000, and an entered forecast of 0 gives 1250000. What does the pair show?
options: The rule floors an entered forecast at the spend plus commitment, and 900000 passed only because it is within tolerance of 940000.
The rule treats 0 as a request to close the line at budget and 900000 as a request to cut scope, so both are honoured.

Any positive entered forecast is taken as typed, even one below the money already spent and committed, where it is flagged, while 0 is not positive and falls back to the larger of budget and spend plus commitment.
The rule reads 900000 as a saving to be booked against the budget, which is why the variance on that line becomes positive at once.
explanation: Positive entries are trusted and marked when they undercut the money already out the door; a zero is no entry, so a descope typed as 0 saves nothing on the report.

prompt: A partner sees OFON-1's cost performance index above 1 on one tile and an overrun of 550000 on another, and suspects one tile is wrong. What should the partner be told?
options: CPI compares earned value from typed progress with actuals to date, while the EAC applies the forecast rule line by line, so CSG-02's spend and CMT-03's entered 1400000 overrun the budget whatever the index says.
They cannot both be right, since CPI above 1 means spend is below earned value and the forecast must then finish under the budget.
CPI includes the commitments of 5000000 and the EAC does not, so the index is flattered by money that has not been spent yet.
The EAC is dated at the end of the window and CPI at the as-of date, so the overrun is expected after 2027-08-15 and not before it.
explanation: DRL-01, CMT-03 and LOG-04 earn more than they spent and carry CPI over 1, while the EAC of 27600000 comes from each line's branch of the one rule.

prompt: CSG-02 is 100.0000 percent complete, with a budget of 3900000 and an actual of 4300000. What does it contribute to OFON-1's earned value?

Its forecast of 4300000, since earned value weights progress by the item forecast once the rule's actual plus commitment branch is taken.
Nothing yet, since earned value counts a line only when its invoices match its actuals, and CSG-02 has spent past the authorised sum.
Its budget, 3900000.
explanation: Earned value pays each line what the work was authorised to cost, so CSG-02 is the one line earning less than it spent, 3900000 against 4300000.

prompt: Write OFON-1's SPI as of 2027-01-15, 2027-08-15 and 2028-01-10. Which triple, with its reasons, is right?

Null before the window opens, where planned value is 0; 0.872063 inside it, earned value 15231500 over planned value 17466060; and 0.563087 after the end, which equals percent complete divided by 100.
Null before the window opens; 1.141290 inside it, since the dashboard reads the planned value of the month the date falls in; and null after the end, when the plan is spent.
0.563087 before the window opens, where the engine falls back to percent complete; 0.872063 inside it; and 0.563087 after the end.

prompt: OFON-1 is re-entered with every actual set to 0 and its progress unchanged, so earned value stays at 15231500. What does the report print for CPI?
options: 1.000000, on budget, since work earned for nothing is read as the cost-neutral index the engine falls back to.
Infinity, since 15231500 over a spend of 0 has no finite value and the engine prints the division as it stands.
The SPI in its place, since with no spend the engine substitutes the schedule index for the cost index on that AFE.
No ratio: CPI is null with cpiStatus "no-spend", and the CPI tile reads N/A with "Nothing spent yet, so no cost efficiency".
explanation: Value earned with nothing spent has no cost efficiency to report, so the engine returns null and names the reason; earned value itself is unchanged by the actuals.

prompt: Why does a graded AFE reading compare the cost lines' actuals with the invoice total before any metric is quoted?
options: Because the engine refuses to compute CPI until the two totals agree, so a mismatch has to be cleared before the dashboard will load its tiles or export a report.
Because the forecast rule reads actual plus commitment from the invoices, so a mismatch changes the EAC and has to be settled before the forecast branches are named.
Because the metrics read the lines and the S-curve reads the invoices, so if the totals differ the two describe different money, and that belongs at the top.
Because the invoice total is the audited figure, and the engine replaces line actuals with it on the as-of date whenever they differ.
explanation: On OFON-1 both read 15090000 because the field was built that way; on a live AFE an accrual on a line or an invoice booked before the line is updated separates them, and an invoice the engine cannot date is kept off the curve and counted beside it.

prompt: A reader takes OFON-1's Nov 27 Forecast, 24949669, as the money the job will spend, and calls the rest of the EAC of 27600000 a saving. What went wrong?
options: Nov 27 is only the last monthly point, standing on the first of November; the curve closes on "30 Nov 27", where Forecast is the EAC of 27600000.
The reader used the Forecast line where the Actual line applies, since past the as-of date the Actual line carries the committed spend to the end.
The reader ignored the as-of date, since the Forecast rises to the EAC only once a report is run after the window's end, when every projected point has become an actual.
Nothing, since the projected line nets the entered forecasts against their budgets and the gap is the saving it has identified.
explanation: The closing point dated the window end carries Forecast 27600000 and Planned 27050000; a reader who stops at the last monthly point sees neither the EAC nor the budget.

prompt: As of 2027-08-15, which of OFON-1's earned value, CPI and SPI can be rebuilt from the S-curve alone?

Earned value, as the Forecast at the as-of date, since the curve projects the work done onto the window from the start.
CPI, as the last Actual over the last Planned point, since both lines are drawn on one budget and share its denominator.
None of them.
explanation: The curve plots no earned value, no point stands on the as-of date, and planned value 17466060 falls between Aug 27 and Sep 27, so SPI 0.872063 and CPI 1.009377 come only from the metrics.

prompt: Two exports of OFON-1 from the Suite agree on an EAC of 27600000 but show different SPIs. Where should the check start?
options: At each line's forecast field, since the exports apply different forecast rules and a copied budget changes SPI.
At the invoices, since the S-curve feeds SPI and a late invoice moves the ratio in one export and not in the other.
At the as-of date each export was run for.
At the progress column, since progress is the only input SPI reads and the EAC agreeing proves the dates were the same.

prompt: A manager says OFON-1 is "55.7856 percent done" and cites its SPI of 0.563087 after the end as agreement. What has been mixed up?
options: Nothing, since SPI after the end is actuals over the budget and both numbers describe spend against the approved figure, read on the same basis at the same date.
55.7856 is percent spent, actuals over budget, while 0.563087 after the end is percent complete 56.3087 divided by 100, work recorded as done.
The manager has quoted CPI as a percentage, since 55.7856 is the cost index scaled by 100 and SPI after the end rounds to it.
The SPI belongs to a report without dates, since an AFE with a window never reports SPI after its end day.
explanation: Percent spent and percent complete share the budget as denominator, and dividing one into the other gives CPI 1.009377; spend is not work.

prompt: The tier ends on the sentence that an AFE report is a forecast rule, a date and the progress typed on the lines. Which pairing of number to input is right?

The EAC rests on the as-of date, earned value on the forecast rule, and SPI on the typed progress alone, since the forecast is dated by the report.
The EAC rests on the typed progress, earned value on the as-of date, and SPI on the forecast rule.
The EAC and earned value rest on the forecast rule, and SPI on the as-of date alone, since progress enters neither the EAC nor the schedule index.
explanation: EAC 27600000 is the rule's branches summed, earned value 15231500 is progress weighted by budget, and SPI 0.872063 divides that earned value by the planned value of 2027-08-15.

prompt: A capstone answer gives OFON-1's planned value at the end of its window as 24452483, read off the Nov 27 point of the S-curve. Where should it have been read?

From the Nov 27 point, which is the plan of record for the whole window.
From the metrics as of 2027-11-30, or the curve's closing point "30 Nov 27", which both give 27050000.
From the metrics as of 2027-08-15, since planned value is fixed on the as-of date and is not carried to the end of the window.

prompt: A committee pack built on a normal approximation quotes -150.5560 as the P90 of a single exploration well that succeeds three times in ten, earns 300 on success and costs 50 on failure. What is wrong with that figure?
options: It was too optimistic, because a well failing 0.700000 of the time has a true low case further down than -150.5560.
It lies beneath -50.0000, the worst outcome the well can produce, so it describes a loss no draw of this project can ever reach.
Nothing of substance, because a low case below the worst outcome only adds a margin a committee reads as conservative.
It carried the wrong label, because under the exceedance convention the low case of that well is its P10.
explanation: A risked project is success or a single failure point, and the bell smooths that gap away; the simulation returns P90 -50.0000, the failure itself.

prompt: Across identical wildcats a normal approximation understates P(loss) with three wells (0.276275 against an exact 0.343000) and overstates it with six (0.200464 against 0.117649). Why can no fixed margin correct the normal figures?
options: The error shrinks steadily as wells are added, so a margin fitted on one well overcorrects every larger portfolio it is applied to.
Only the P90 error changes sign between three and six wells, so a margin would repair the probabilities and leave the low cases wrong.
The approximation turns exact once six wells are funded, so only smaller portfolios need a margin.
The error changes sign as wells are added, so nothing tells a reviewer which way to lean on a given portfolio.
explanation: With eight wells it understates again, 0.166046 against 0.255298, so the direction of the error follows the lumps of the outcomes.

prompt: In one simulated iteration OKONO's OK-3 (pos 0.250000, npv_p50 420.0000, fail cost 85.0000) fails. What does the risk simulation book for it?
options: A loss of exactly 85.0000 with no spread, since its success spread of 191.1747 scales z2 only when the project succeeds.
Its npv_p90 of 210.0000, the low percentile of its entered range, booked as the downside of a poor outcome.
A loss drawn around 85.0000 on its mixture sd of 238.6507, so a single failure can cost a little more or a little less than entered.
Its risked EMV of 41.2500, because the simulation books each project's expected value in every iteration.
explanation: A failure is one number, booked in about three iterations out of four; the mixture sd feeds only the closed-form stdDev and is never drawn.

prompt: An analyst reruns OKONO's 450.0000 set, the same OK-1, OK-3 and OK-4, at seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations, but enters them as OK-4, OK-3, OK-1. P(loss) moves off 0.123600. What happened?
options: Project order decides which project hears the shared drivers F1 and F2, so the reordered set was simulated under a different correlation.
Entering OK-4 first made its fail cost the threshold for every draw, so losses were counted from another zero.
The normals were dealt to the projects in a different order, so the same set at the same seed moved by sampling noise alone.
A seeded run is meant to ignore how the list is typed, so a result that moves with the input order is a defect in the engine.
explanation: Each iteration draws F1, F2, then e1 and e2 per project in array order, so reproducing 0.123600 needs the seed, the iterations and the project order.

prompt: A risk review calls two portfolios equally dangerous because both lose money about as often: identical6 at an exact 0.117649, OKONO's funded 450.0000 set at a simulated 0.123600. What does the pairing show?
options: That the two portfolios hold about the same downside, because an equal loss probability places their low cases at the same percentile of simulated NPV.
P(loss) says how often and never how much: every identical6 loss is -300.0000, while the 450.0000 set reads a P90 of only -18.3574.
That identical6 is the safer, because its losses need all six wells to fail and a joint failure costs less than a partial one.
Nothing usable, because a binary portfolio's loss probability cannot be set beside one with a success spread.
explanation: identical6 loses only when all six wells fail, so its loss is the floor itself; a loss probability has to be read beside the low case.

prompt: identical8's engine P90 is -50.0000. A reviewer writes it up as the worst this eight-well portfolio can do. What is the correction?
options: The label is swapped: -50.0000 is the high case P10 under the exceedance convention, so the low case is elsewhere.
The sample is too small: 10000 iterations cannot reach an outcome beyond the exact P90, so the worst case of eight wells is unknown to the engine.
None is needed, because on a lumpy portfolio the engine reports the minimum simulated outcome as its P90.
P90 is the 10th percentile of simulated NPV, here one success and seven failures, and all eight wells failing loses more.
explanation: The engine reports no minimum, so the worst outcome, every well failing at 50.0000, is written by hand beside the P90.

prompt: On mixtureWithSpread a normal approximation puts P90 at -12.4175 and the simulation reads 1.7148. What would a reader of the normal figure conclude wrongly?
options: That the low case loses money, when nine outcomes in ten are at or above a small gain.
That -12.4175 was the very worst the portfolio could do, when the simulation shows its worst outcome is a gain of 1.7148.
That the portfolio was lumpy, when a success spread makes the outcomes continuous and the normal approximation exact on such a case.
That the high case was a gain, when the committee should have read P10 first because it is the low case under exceedance.
explanation: The exact P90 outcome is 1.5838, so the sign of the low case changed with the method; the normal approximation is exact only on the pos1-normal cases.

prompt: At rho 0.000000 OKONO's 600.0000 set prints emv 402.7500 and stdDev 143.8374. A reviewer derives its low case as emv - 1.2816 x stdDev. Why does that disagree with the reported P90 of 200.3575?
options: The multiplier belongs to P10, so the low case needs emv plus 1.2816 x stdDev, and the reviewer has quoted the high tail.
The engine derives P90 from the closed-form stdDev only when rho is above 0, and at rho 0 it switches to a separate formula.
That shortcut is a normal approximation, 218.4079 here, while the reported P90 is counted from simulated draws of success and failure.
It does not disagree in substance, because at rho 0 the closed form and the simulation are the same model and the gap is sampling noise.
explanation: At 300.0000 the same shortcut gives 108.3959 against a simulated 100.7698; a bell on a risked set misses the low case in either direction.

prompt: An analyst has a historical figure for how often two prospects in one basin succeed and fail in step, and enters that event correlation directly as rho. How does the risk summary come out?
options: Too alarming a P(loss) and P90, because rho acts on outcomes and a measured correlation of successes already includes the size of each success.
Too comfortable a P(loss) and P90, because rho correlates the latent drivers and the event correlation it produces is lower.
The same figures as the right input, because the engine converts an event correlation into a driver correlation.
A lower emv, because a correlation typed from observed outcomes pulls each project's chance of success down.
explanation: Between 0 and 1 the event correlation is less than rho, so the measured figure understates the drivers; at rho 1 three identical wildcats fail together, exact P(loss) 0.700000.

prompt: A team enters a negative correlation to represent two projects that hedge each other. What does the portfolio engine do with it?
options: Refuses it with a PortfolioInputError and returns no risk summary, exactly as it refuses a negative capex before any set is built.
Returns the full risk summary marked invalid with an engine note, the way a negative working interest returns valid false.
Takes its magnitude, because the sign of a correlation only decides which tail the shared driver pushes and the spread is the same.
Clamps it to 0.000000 and simulates the projects as independent, so no hedge can be represented.
explanation: The published clampBelow case uses correlation 0.000000 and stdDev 60.9438, the rho 0 figure; a correlation is clamped, where a capex is refused and a share is flagged.

prompt: A reviewer checks the stdDev of OKONO's 600.0000 set at rho 1 by adding the four projects' success spreads. Why does the check fall short of 239.8888?
options: The formula uses mixture sds, which carry the gap between success and failure; OK-4 alone is 121.9467 against a success spread of 78.0305.
Adding standard deviations is the rho 0 end of the formula, and at rho 1 the engine adds the variances and takes the square root instead.
The engine applies rho to the latent drivers, so its stdDev at rho 1 always runs above the plain sum of whichever sds are added.
The closed form counts each cross term twice over, so its figure at rho 1 exceeds any plain sum of the four spreads by construction.
explanation: At rho 1 stdDev is sqrt(57546.6428) = 239.8888, exactly 44.3821 + 60.6850 + 121.9467 + 12.8750 added like money.

prompt: identical3, copulaIdentical3 and comonotoneIdentical3 hold the same three wells. Exact P(loss) runs 0.343000, 0.469561 and 0.700000, yet the exact P90 outcome is -150.0000 on every row. Why?
options: The low case of a binary portfolio is set by the fail costs alone and never reads pos, so correlation cannot move it on any portfolio.
Correlation moves the spread and never the mean, and on a portfolio of binary wells the low case is part of what the mean fixes.
All three failing together is at least 0.343000 likely on every row, more than one draw in ten, so the 10th percentile already sits on that floor.
The copula and comonotone rows were published with the P90 column copied from the independent row, since the exact percentile was not solved.
explanation: On OKONO's 600.0000 set no lump is that likely, and its P90 falls from 200.3575 to 87.9316 as rho rises from 0 to 1.

prompt: A committee leaves rho at its default for OK-1, OK-2, OK-4 and OK-5 and reports P(loss) 0.001800. What has it asserted about the projects?
options: Nothing about them, since the default is neutral and the engine replaces it with the correlation implied by the inventory's own spreads.
That the four share no reservoir, no price and no operator, the most optimistic dependence the engine accepts.
That they hedge one another, which is why the default gives the lowest loss probability.
Only that the sizes of their successes are independent, since rho acts on the success spread and leaves the chance of success to pos.
explanation: rho 0 is independence and the floor of the clamp; the same set reads P(loss) 0.059000 at rho 1.000000, so choosing rho is choosing the answer.

prompt: A committee raises rho to 1.000000 at the 600.0000 limit, watches P90 drop to 87.9316 and P(loss) reach 0.059000, and expects the engine to swap in a safer set. What does the optimizer fund?
options: OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 + OK-5, trading risked EMV for a set that the shared driver ties together less tightly than the waterflood and compression.
A set with fewer large projects, because once correlation is above the default the optimizer charges each project's stdDev against its EMV.
OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4, the 450.0000 optimum, because the frontier is rebuilt at each correlation and its sets are not nested across budgets.
OK-1 + OK-2 + OK-4 + OK-5, as at every rho, because rho reaches only the risk summary.
explanation: The optimizer maximises summed risked EMV, which is 402.7500 at every rho; a committee that wants a narrower low case compares sets by hand.

prompt: Between rho 0.000000 and 1.000000 the 600.0000 set's P10 rises from 580.5960 to 674.8353. How should that rise be read?
options: As the same widening seen from the high tail: a shared driver brings good iterations together as surely as bad ones.
As an upside to bank, since P10 is the low case under exceedance and its rise cuts the downside.
As a gain in value offsetting the fall in P90, so that the expected outcome of the set stays level only by coincidence at this budget.
As sampling noise, since correlation only pushes the low tail and a moving high tail is the seed.
explanation: P90 falls from 200.3575 to 87.9316 over the same range while emv holds at 402.7500, the one figure correlation cannot touch.

prompt: In the Suite an analyst wants OKONO's 600.0000 set at full dependence and drags the correlation slider to its top. What does the screen show?
options: The rho 1.000000 figures, because the slider runs over the engine's full range of correlation from 0 to 1.
An engine refusal, because the engine clamps correlation at 0.9 and throws for any value above it.
The rho 0.900000 figures, stdDev 232.0795 and P(loss) 0.049500, because the Suite's slider stops at 0.9.
The rho 1.000000 figures under a flag, since the slider's top is labelled 0.9 but passes the clamped maximum of 1 through to the engine.
explanation: The engine accepts 1 and reads stdDev 239.8888 and P(loss) 0.059000 there; the slider's top is the app's limit on what can be set from the screen.

prompt: An analyst sends Ofon Energy, at 40.0000 percent of OFON-1, a bill of 10820000 today. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing, because a working interest is a share of the approved cost and the budget of 27050000 is exactly the cost the partners approved.
10820000 is the share of the budget, an authorisation; on the actuals to date of 15090000 the same interest bills 6036000.
The party is wrong: 10820000 is the operator's residual, and Ofon Energy owes 6762500 today.
It should be split on the EAC of 27600000, since a partner is billed its share of the forecast final cost once the AFE is approved.
explanation: The interest does not change between the two totals, only the total does, and the four bills on actuals sum to 15090000.

prompt: Ofon Energy asks for its share of OFON-1's final exposure, for its own planning. Which total should its 40.0000 percent be applied to?
options: The budget of 27050000, because every line with no entered forecast forecasts its budget and the final exposure therefore equals the budget share.
The actuals plus the commitments of 5000000, because orders already placed become the partner's final exposure once they are invoiced.
The actuals of 15090000, because a working interest applies only to money spent and a forecast of the remainder is the operator's concern.
The EAC of 27600000, a forecast by one rule, used for planning and never put on an invoice.
explanation: CSG-02 forecasts its actual of 4300000 and CMT-03 its entered 1400000, which is why the variance at completion is -550000; bills split the actuals to date.

prompt: The OFON-1 partner list is keyed in with Ofon Energy and Enang Petroleum only, and Mfem Resources with its 12.5000 percent is left off by mistake. What does the split return?
options: valid true with no note, while the operator's residual silently absorbs Mfem's 12.5000 percent of every bill.
valid false with a note that the interests fall short of the whole, because a shortfall is flagged in the same way as a total over it.
A refusal naming the missing partner, checked against the joint operating agreement.
valid true with the operator held at 25.0000 percent and the missing 12.5000 percent left unbilled until someone enters the partner.
explanation: The published 10 percent shortfall reads valid true with the operator at 90.0000; there is no field for the operator's own interest, so the check is by hand.

prompt: On the published split at 70 and 45 percent of a cost of 1000.00, the two partner amounts and the operator's add back to 1000.00. What does that reconciliation prove?
options: That the allocation can be billed, because amounts that sum to the cost are how the engine defines valid.
That the engine rescaled the interests to the whole before allocating, so the amounts come back to the cost.
Nothing about the split, since the operator's -150.00 restores the sum; valid false and the partner total of 115.00 percent catch it.
That only the operator's figure needs editing to 0 percent, after which the partners' 700.00 and 450.00 can be billed as they stand.
explanation: The note says the interests total 115.00 percent and the operator share is negative; the fix belongs in the partner list; the computed operator figure is left alone.

prompt: Partner interests of 30 and -20 percent on a cost of 1000.00 leave the operator 90.0000 percent, a share that is not negative. Why does the engine still mark the split valid false?
options: It zeroes the negative interest first, finds the operator at 70 percent, and flags the gap between that and the 90.0000 it was handed.
It checks every partner interest as well as the operator residual, and its note names Partner "B" at -20.00 percent.
It compares the partner amounts with the cost, and a credit of -200.00 leaves the amounts short of the 1000.00 total.
It reads a negative interest as a carry, and a carry has to be entered in a field the split does not have.
explanation: A partner total of 10 percent leaves the residual positive, so a test on the operator share alone would pass this split; the note reads "Partner "B" has a negative working interest (-20.00 percent). Correct the interests before billing."

prompt: The AFE split flags a negative working interest, while the portfolio engine refuses a negative capex. What separates the two behaviours?
options: Nothing in effect, because a flagged split also withholds every amount until the interests are corrected and the split is run again.
The flag clamps the negative interest to 0 and allocates the rest, while the refusal throws only because a capex has no safe clamp.
The refusal fires on large errors such as -150 and the flag on small ones, so a capex of -0.5 would also be allocated with a warning.
The refusal returns no set, frontier or risk summary; the flag returns the whole allocation with valid false and a note, so the error can be traced.
explanation: -0.5 is refused as firmly as -150, while interests of 30 and -20 still show the operator at 900.00 beside the engine note.

prompt: OFON-1's line actuals and its S-curve's last Actual point both read 15090000, and a biller splits whichever is to hand. When would the S-curve total bill partners on the wrong amount?
options: When an invoice cannot be dated, since the curve leaves it out and only the count beside the curve names it.
When a line carries an entered forecast, which the curve's Actual line then follows.
When commitments are open, since the curve adds orders placed to each Actual point while the cost lines hold commitments apart.
Never, because the engine reconciles invoices to the line actuals before drawing the curve and refuses an AFE on which they differ.
explanation: In the published undated case neither invoice reaches the curve, whose Actual reads 0, and the engine reports 2 undated invoices; a bill should name which actuals it split.

prompt: A project with npv_p50 80 and fail_cost 30 is typed with pos 1.4. What does the portfolio engine do?
options: Reads pos as 1 and returns risked EMV 80.0000, with nothing on the result to say the input changed.
Uses 1.4 as typed, so the risked EMV exceeds the success-case NPV and the project ranks above every certain project in the inventory.
Refuses it with a PortfolioInputError naming the project: "has a pos outside 0 to 1 (1.4); pos must be a number from 0 to 1".
Marks the project invalid and funds it anyway, the way the partner split returns its allocation beside valid false.
explanation: The published posAboveOneRefused case carries the same message; a chance of success is a probability, so 1.4 has no reading the engine could take, and -0.2 is refused the same way.

prompt: To get past the message that Project B has a negative capex (-150), an analyst types 0 in its place. What has the analyst made?
options: A project the optimizer can never fund, because a capex of 0 leaves its EMV per million USD undefined and the solve drops it.
A free project, funded whenever its EMV is positive, with whatever the negative number carried, such as a receipt, gone from the model.
A second refusal, since a capex of exactly 0 is read as a missing capex and throws another error.
The same project with its receipt kept, because a refused capex is booked into the NPV first.
explanation: In freeProjectTightLimit a free project with EMV 10.0000 rides beside A at capex 100.0000 under a limit of 100.0000, and the engine funds free + A for 70.0000; the receipt belonged in the NPV.

prompt: An engineer wants CSG-02, at 100.0000 percent with actuals of 4300000 against a budget of 3900000, to show more earned value and types its progress as 110. What happens to OFON-1's report?
options: Earned value rises by a tenth of CSG-02's budget, lifting CPI above 1.009377 with nothing on the report to mark the entry.
CSG-02 is read at 100 percent and the report carries on unchanged, since progress past the whole is capped quietly.
The line is flagged beside the metrics, the way a negative working interest is flagged beside the allocation.
No report comes back: the AFE engine throws for that line, and the metrics return only once it is corrected.
explanation: Progress runs from 0 to 100 percent and a value outside that range is refused by line; CSG-02 at 100.0000 percent already earns its whole budget.

prompt: An as-of date of 30 February is refused on an AFE that has no window, where time progress falls back to 1.000000 and the date would move nothing. Why refuse it?
options: A lenient parser would roll it into March and report on a day nobody chose, so every invalid as-of date is refused first.
Because an AFE with no window reads SPI from the as-of date alone, so a bad date would misplace the plan.
Because 30 February is read as the start day, where SPI is null, and a report with no SPI is declined.
Because an invalid date would set time progress to 1 on an AFE with no window, and the engine blocks that fallback.
explanation: The published case throws "asOf is not a valid date" with no AFE dates; negative progress throws the same way, returning no metrics at all.

prompt: Under a limit of 6000.0000 the published gridOvershoot case offers A (capex 4000.0000, EMV 500.0000), B (2002.0000, 300.0000) and C (1995.0000, 280.0000). A + B would return 800.0000. What does the optimizer fund?
options: A + B at 800.0000, since 2.0000 over the limit is inside one grid cell and the engine counts that as within the limit.
A + B with overLimit true and overLimitBy 2.0000, leaving the committee to trim 2.0000 of capex from the higher EMV.
A + C at capex 5995.0000 for 780.0000, solved exactly with overLimit false, since A + B does not fit the limit.
A alone at 500.0000, since a set that would break the limit is discarded and the largest single project that fits is kept.
explanation: The result reads solveMethod exact and optimalityGap 0.0000; ranking 800.0000 against 780.0000 would prefer a set the budget cannot pay for.

prompt: Called with exactStateLimit 3, the published gridUndershootFallback case funds X + Y + Z at 660.0000 with overLimit false and optimalityGap 200.0000. What do the two readings tell the reader?
options: That the set is the best within the limit, since overLimit false is raised only when the fallback matches the exact optimum.
That 200.0000 of the limit was left unspent, since optimalityGap reports the capex the rounded-up grid could not use.
That W was rightly dropped, since its EMV of 200.0000 is the lowest of the four and the gap names the project left out.
overLimit false says only that the set fits; the gap bounds what a better set could add, and the exact solve funds all four at 860.0000.
explanation: Every weight is rounded up, to 500, 500, 500 and 501 cells against 2000, so the four cannot fit the grid together; rounded down they fit, and 860.0000 less 660.0000 is the gap.

prompt: Which of these is a property the course teaches as it stands in the engines and the Suite?
options: SPI reported as Infinity before the start date when value has already been earned.
Time progress 1 on an AFE with no dates, so SPI there measures nothing and the Suite labels it unavailable.
A P90 read off a normal curve that sits beneath the worst outcome of a single wildcat.
An S-curve that keeps walking past its end date to the current month.
explanation: The published no-dates case reads time progress 1.000000 and SPI 0.250000; SPI is null before and on the start day, the risk summary is simulated, and the S-curve closes on a point dated the window end.

prompt: Suppose OFON-1's cost postings are wiped so every line shows zero spend while progress stays as typed, and CPI now prints null with cpiStatus "no-spend". As of 2027-08-15, which reading keeps both its value and its meaning?
options: SPI 0.872063, because earned value ignores actuals and planned value comes from the calendar.
The EAC of 27600000, because the forecast rule reads budgets and entered forecasts and never looks at the actuals on a line.
The variance at completion of -550000, because a zero actual moves only the S-curve's Actual line and none of the metrics.
CPI itself, because a null CPI reads as exactly on budget whenever nothing has been spent on the lines.
explanation: SPI is 15231500 over 17466060; CSG-02 forecast from its actual of 4300000, so zeroing the actuals does move the EAC.

prompt: The published empty AFE, with no lines, no progress and no spend, is read for its CPI and SPI. What does the engine report?
options: CPI 1.000000 and SPI 1.000000, exactly on cost and on schedule, since both ratios equal one when nothing has happened.
CPI null with cpiStatus "no-spend" and SPI 0.000000, since a budget of 0 plans nothing and so earns against nothing.
An AfeInputError, since an AFE with no lines cannot be measured and is refused before any ratio is formed.
CPI null with cpiStatus "no-spend" and SPI null with spiStatus "no-budget": neither ratio can be formed.
explanation: A reported ratio carries the status "ok"; here there is no spend to divide by and no budget to plan, and the Suite's SPI tile reads "N/A" with "No budget to measure schedule against".

prompt: An S-curve reads Planned 0 and Actual 0 at its first point, and 2 undated invoices are reported beside it. What is the Actual line leaving out?
options: Only the invoice whose invoice_date is null, because one with no invoice_date field is placed on the start day of the window instead.
Nothing at all, because the count is a display note and both amounts are still carried into every bucket from the window's start day.
Every invoice the engine could not date, since none of them reaches a bucket at all.
The commitments, because the curve's Actual line adds the orders placed at the start of the window and drops them again once they are invoiced.
explanation: In the published undated case the Actual reads 0 at Jan 20 and at the closing point 31 Dec 20 while the engine reports 2 undated invoices; a dated invoice first shows at the first point on or after its date.

prompt: OFON-1 is read as of its end day, 2027-11-30. Its metrics give planned value 27050000, while the chart's Nov 27 point shows 24452483. Which figure is the plan?
options: The Nov 27 point, because the 2597517 after it is contingency the plan never meant to spend.
The planned value in the metrics, 27050000, the same figure the chart shows at its window-end point.
The Nov 27 point, because the metrics read the plan from the budget while the curve builds it from invoices, the better record.
Neither, because SPI is null on the end day and planned value is undefined once the window has closed.
explanation: Monthly points sit on the 1st, so Nov 27 falls a month early; the chart's last point is dated the end day and carries the whole budget.

prompt: A project manager stops at the last monthly point of OFON-1's chart, "Nov 27", sees Forecast 24949669 under the 27050000 authorisation, and tells the partners the well will come in cheap. What is the correction?
options: After the as-of date the Forecast line continues from the actual spend of 15090000, so 24949669 is the honest projection of the remaining work.
The curve plots only budgets after the as-of date, so CMT-03's 1400000 is missing.
The chart draws one EAC rule and the metrics another, so the curve forecasts from the budget and the manager's reading stands.
Read the chart to its end: on the window-end point the forecast is 27600000 beside a plan of 27050000, an overrun of 550000.
explanation: After the as-of date Forecast is the EAC spread from the start, jumping from 15090000 to 19374834, and it reaches the EAC on the point dated 30 Nov 27.

prompt: OKONO's 450.0000 set reads P(loss) 0.123600 at seed 20260829 with a standard error of 0.003291, where a normal approximation gives 0.142035. A reviewer proposes 40000 iterations to settle which is right. What will the run settle?
options: Only the simulation's own precision, 0.125975 with a standard error of 0.001659; the gap to 0.142035 is a different model, which no iteration count closes.
Which model is right, because as iterations grow the simulated count converges on the normal approximation and the gap closes.
Nothing at all, because the larger run reuses the default seed and so repeats the draws of the 10000 iteration run exactly.
That the normal approximation is nearer the truth, since 0.125975 sits closer to 0.142035 than 0.123600 did and the trend runs toward it.
explanation: The published cases sit no further than 1.4289 standard errors from exact, while a normal approximation misses the single wildcat's 0.700000 by dozens.
